## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

_How much autonomy can an embodied machine legitimately hold when empirical evidence cannot settle every premise upon which its safety depends?_

As Physical AI systems advance from structured industrial automation toward open-world autonomy—operating alongside human beings in unstructured homes, crowded public spaces, and safety-critical infrastructure—they encounter an inescapable epistemic boundary. In disembodied machine learning systems, an unmodeled edge case or out-of-distribution input results in a misclassified image, a degraded recommendation ranking, or an ungrounded hallucination in a web browser. In embodied physical systems, however, software commands kinetic energy, mechanical momentum, and high-voltage motor currents across a continuous causal boundary. Here, a computational failure does not terminate with an unhandled exception or an error log entry; it manifests as plastic metal deformation, mechanical fracture, or catastrophic human trauma governed by the conservation laws of Newtonian physics.

No finite volume of physical testing, no simulation suite however massive, and no formal verification proof can ever anticipate every combinatorial variation of an open physical world. Real-world environments are inherently open, non-stationary, and governed by extreme-value heavy tails of human behavior and rare physical transitions. When an autonomous system operates beyond the certified perimeter of its operational design domain, how must its architecture behave?

This concluding chapter synthesizes the four-part intellectual journey of this book, establishing why Physical AI is fundamentally an architectural discipline uniting unprivileged statistical proposals from large foundation models with deterministic real-time enforcers, formal safety shields, and hardware interlocks. Across this book, we have analyzed how moving mass commits kinetic momentum, how embedded batch-1 streaming inference bounds compute, how closed-loop rollouts induce endogenous distribution shifts, and how cryptographically signed release manifests govern deployment. Here, we examine the open research frontiers of physical foundation models, lifelong continuous adaptation, and self-supervised world modeling, while directly confronting the hard theoretical and physical boundaries of epistemic unobservability, extreme-value distributions, and finite empirical exposure. True frontier engineering in Physical AI does not pursue the dangerous illusion of unconstrained statistical omniscience; it constructs verifiable systems architectures that explicitly bound unprivileged statistical proposals, enforce deterministic physical invariants, and accountably derate or refuse operational authority when unverified physical premises are breached.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Assess which safety claims exceed the empirical evidence available for a specific physical machine
- Evaluate whether a runtime detector can identify an impending hazard before effective physical intervention becomes impossible
- Construct residual-claims register entries, each with an active operating restriction, an accountable owner, and a sized empirical closure test
- Classify an open safety premise by the missing observable, evaluation deficit, theoretical deficit, or scope mismatch that would close it
- Trace the four bedrock laws through an unfamiliar physical machine and isolate which operational premise of each remains open

:::

## Epistemic Limits {#sec-frontier-epistemic-limits}

Every engineering method has an epistemic boundary where its formal guarantees expire. In physical AI, that boundary is not merely an algorithmic shortfall; it is a physical confrontation between compute latency, sensory observability, and mechanical inertia. Scaling the parameter count of foundation models can yield extraordinary semantic breadth, but it cannot bend the laws of motion: as networks grow, inference latency expands the reaction corridor, trading agility for deliberative depth. Physical AI is therefore fundamentally an architectural discipline: it unites unprivileged statistical proposals from deep neural networks with deterministic real-time enforcers and hardware interlocks operating at high frequency on dedicated, isolated silicon. To navigate this frontier, systems engineers must confront two fundamental limits: the physical coupling of computational delay and thermal constraints to mechanical motion, and the insurmountable divide between stochastic sensor noise and unobservable physical state.

### Embodied latency scaling and thermal dissipation ceilings {#sec-frontier-latency-thermal-scaling}

In modern deep learning, the empirical paradigm of neural scaling laws [@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022chinchilla] demonstrates that expanding model parameter counts, training compute, and dataset tokens systematically drives down loss and unlocks emergent semantic capabilities. In disembodied software environments, the trade-off of scaling is purely computational: evaluating a 70-billion-parameter foundation model may consume hundreds of milliseconds per token, but that turnaround delay affects only the user interface without altering the truth value or physical safety of the generated text.

In physical AI, however, this classical scaling thesis collides directly with an inescapable physical boundary. When an autonomous machine moves mass through a shared operational workspace, time is not an abstract software profiling metric—it is a physical state variable governed by Newtonian kinematics. In data center serving infrastructure, high token throughput is achieved by batching hundreds of concurrent requests ($B \ge 64$), amortizing weight memory transfers across queries and operating deep within the compute-bound regime of the roofline model. In embedded robotics, however, closed-loop control demands streaming batch size 1 ($B = 1$) to minimize latency. Under batch-1 execution, arithmetic intensity collapses to $\approx 1\text{ FLOP/byte}$, pinning inference execution strictly against the hardware memory wall ($f \le B_{\text{mem}} / M$, @sec-brain-memory-wall). Every weight matrix must be streamed from off-chip DRAM to on-chip SRAM for every single forward pass. For an 8-billion-parameter foundation model in 16-bit precision, streaming $16\text{ GB}$ of weights across an embedded system-on-chip (SoC) memory bus rated at $204.8\text{ GB/s}$ imposes a rigid physical latency floor of at least $t_{\text{inf}} \ge 16\text{ GB} / 204.8\text{ GB/s} \approx 78\text{ ms}$, entirely before accounting for attention key-value (KV) cache memory traffic, activation movement, or token projection. Every additional parameter, attention head, and transformer layer that inflates inference latency directly expands the machine's unbraked reaction corridor ($d_{\text{blind}} = v \cdot t_{\text{inference}}$). If computational deliberation stretches reaction time beyond available spatial clearance, increasing neural capacity directly degrades dynamic stability and mechanical safety.

This fundamental coupling between neural capacity, computational delay, and kinetic momentum is formalized in the **embodied latency scaling law** (\ref{dfn-frontier-embodied-latency-scaling-law}).

::: {#dfn-frontier-embodied-latency-scaling-law .callout-definition title="Embodied latency scaling law"}

***Embodied latency scaling law***\index{Embodied latency scaling law!definition}\index{Scaling laws!embodied latency} is the physical constraint dictating that scaling neural policy parameter count yields diminishing operational safety returns unless inference latency decreases proportionally, because physical reaction distance $d_{\text{react}} = v \cdot (t_{\text{inference}} + t_{\text{actuation}}) + \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\max}}$ scales linearly with computational delay.

1.  **Significance**: Establishes that intelligence in physical systems cannot be scaled purely by adding model parameters, because computational delay directly degrades dynamic stability and spatial stopping clearance.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike compute scaling laws in static language modeling where latency affects only token generation speed, embodied latency scaling directly couples computational delay to mechanical reaction time constants ($t_{\text{react}} \ge t_{\text{inference}} + t_{\text{actuation}}$).
3.  **Common pitfall**: Deploying multi-billion parameter foundation models directly in the closed-loop control path under the assumption that greater semantic reasoning compensates for an unbudgeted response delay.

:::

This tension, codified in \ref{dfn-frontier-embodied-latency-scaling-law}, illustrates why parameter scaling alone cannot solve real-time safety. In natural language processing or visual generation, an offboard foundation model can scale to hundreds of billions of parameters because queuing delay and token generation latency affect only user-perceived turnaround time. In physical AI, offloading inference to edge servers across wireless networks introduces network transport latency and jitter ($t_{\text{comm}} = 50\text{ ms} \pm 30\text{ ms}$). If a mobile manipulator evaluates an 8-billion-parameter Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy with an offboard inference latency of $t_{\text{inf}} = 200\text{ ms}$, the total computational and communication delay inflates blind travel by:
$$d_{\text{blind, offboard}} = v \cdot (t_{\text{inf}} + t_{\text{comm}}) = 1.3\text{ m/s} \times (0.200\text{ s} + 0.050\text{ s}) = 325\text{ mm}.$$
This single latency increment exhausts the entire $102.6\text{ mm}$ spare margin of the warehouse aisle (@sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes) more than threefold before the brakes can even begin building hydraulic pressure.

Furthermore, while cloud foundation models scale compute by drawing megawatts across liquid-cooled data center racks, physical AI is bounded by the **chassis thermal dissipation ceiling**\index{Compute scaling!chassis thermal dissipation}. A warehouse mobile manipulator or humanoid robot operates within an IP65 dust- and moisture-sealed enclosure, constraining continuous onboard compute power to a strict $15\text{ to }60\,\text{W}$ thermal envelope (the operating regime of embedded system-on-chip accelerators such as NVIDIA Jetson Orin). Dissipating more than $60\text{ to }100\,\text{W}$ within a sealed mobile chassis demands bulky heat sinks, radiator loops, or forced-air cooling ducts that ingest ambient warehouse dust and fail under continuous shock and vibration. Exceeding this thermal envelope triggers silicon thermal throttling ($T_j \ge 105^\circ\text{C}$), which stretches clock cycles, degrades inference frame rates, and directly violates real-time reaction budgets. Physical AI cannot simply compute its way through epistemic limits by deploying data-center-scale neural networks onboard.

The contrast between disembodied compute scaling and embodied physical scaling exposes a fundamental divergence in systems engineering. In disembodied foundation models, the Chinchilla scaling paradigm [@hoffmann2022chinchilla] dictates that cross-entropy loss scales as a power law with training FLOPs and dataset tokens ($\mathcal{L}(C) \propto C^{-\alpha}$). Cloud data centers scale tokens by scraping petabytes of static web text, distributing optimization across tens of thousands of liquid-cooled accelerators over high-bandwidth Infiniband fabrics. In Physical AI, however, intelligence must scale across real-world physical interactions, where the scaling frontier is governed by the **Physical Action Scaling Law** and the **Physical Entropy Bottleneck**:

1. **Wall-clock temporal binding**: Web tokens are disembodied bits that can be generated or processed at millions of tokens per second. Physical actions, however, are strictly bound by the arrow of physical time: collecting one hour of physical manipulation or locomotion trajectory requires exactly one hour of physical wall-clock time ($T_{\text{fleet}} = N_{\text{robots}} \cdot t_{\text{wallclock}}$). Physical interaction cannot be accelerated beyond the physical dynamics of the robot and environment without fundamentally altering contact forces, inertia, and aerodynamics.
2. **Mechanical wear and physical entropy**: In cloud training, failed gradient updates or out-of-distribution inputs cost only wasted electrical energy; the GPU state is reset with a software interrupt. In physical AI, however, rollouts extract a permanent mechanical tax: gear tooth pitting and backlash in harmonic and cycloidal drives, thermal degradation of copper motor winding insulation, and wear across elastomeric tactile fingertip skins (such as GelSight or DIGIT sensors). When a trial fails under high kinetic energy, the physical plant suffers plastic deformation, link fracture, or destruction of surrounding infrastructure.
3. **Data distribution entropy and non-ergodicity**: Web text is largely stationary and amenable to offline curation. Physical interaction data is non-ergodic and non-stationary: ambient lighting shifts, mechanical joints loosen over thousands of cycles, floor surfaces accumulate micro-films of dust and moisture, and human coworkers introduce unmodeled reactive behaviors. Physical AI systems cannot simply scale their way to dependability by accumulating more nominal hours; they must contend with the physical entropy of the real world.

### Aleatoric noise vs. epistemic unobservability {#sec-frontier-aleatoric-vs-epistemic}

Beyond computational and thermal ceilings, systems engineers must separate two fundamentally distinct classes of operational uncertainty when bounding autonomous authority:

1. **Aleatoric uncertainty**\index{Uncertainty!aleatoric vs. epistemic}: Stochastic variability inherent in physical sensors and dynamic environments—such as photon shot noise in CMOS image sensors, thermal Johnson-Nyquist noise in MEMS accelerometers, or high-frequency tire slip over rough aggregate. Because aleatoric noise is conditionally zero-mean and stationary, recursive state estimators (such as extended Kalman filters, particle filters, or spatial Gaussian splats) can integrate measurements over time to filter out the variance, achieving asymptotic noise cancellation proportional to $1/\sqrt{N}$ governed by the Central Limit Theorem.
2. **Epistemic uncertainty**\index{Epistemic uncertainty!physical unobservability}: Systematic ignorance arising from unmodeled dynamics, out-of-distribution environments, or physically unobservable state variables. A clear film of hydraulic oil on concrete produces optical reflection and absorption characteristics that are indistinguishable from dry concrete under ambient lighting ($y_A \equiv y_B$). Here, the physical observation operator $g: \mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{Y}$ is non-injective ($g(S_{\text{dry}}) = g(S_{\text{oil}}) \equiv y$). Unlike aleatoric noise, **epistemic blindness cannot be averaged away**: capturing 1,000 consecutive camera frames at 30 Hz yields 1,000 identical, ambiguous measurements. By the Data Processing Inequality, the mutual information across the physical transduction channel is zero ($\mathcal{I}(S; Y) = 0$), guaranteeing that downstream neural representations carry zero information ($\mathcal{I}(S; Z) = 0$). No amount of statistical filtering, recursive Bayesian factor graph estimation, or latent autoencoder projection can uncover a state that the physics of transduction does not register.

This epistemic unobservability extends directly to high-dexterity tactile manipulation and whole-body dynamic locomotion. When a multi-fingered robotic hand grasps a deformable or slick object, the friction coefficient $\mu$ is not an invariant scalar; under classical Coulomb-Amontons friction and Cattaneo-Mindlin contact mechanics, the contact interface transitions through complex non-uniform shear stress distributions. A thin film of lubricant, localized surface wear, or internal fluid sloshing inside a non-rigid container generates an epistemic blind spot: optical vision observing external geometry registers completely stationary boundaries, while at the microscopic contact patch, shear displacement is already propagating toward catastrophic slip. Unless the robot possesses high-bandwidth, high-density optical or piezoresistive tactile arrays measuring micro-vibrations ($> 500\text{ Hz}$) and elastomeric marker displacement, incipient slip remains completely unobservable until the object is already in free fall under gravity.

As governed by Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety [@ashby1956introduction], a controller cannot regulate disturbances that its sensory architecture cannot perceive. When an unmodeled disturbance enters the physical plant, no amount of latent computation can compensate for missing physical evidence.

A pallet jack with a weeping hydraulic line crosses one aisle of the site where the warehouse mobile manipulator works, and it leaves a clear film of fluid on the concrete. The machine's stopping budget assumes that the floor can supply the friction its credible deceleration needs, and on dry concrete it can. Under the film it may not, and neither the navigation camera nor the lidar can tell the film from dry floor. The permission path can meet every deadline, the chunk lease can expire on time, and the brake can engage on schedule while the stop still runs past the rack end, because the term that failed is a premise that no sensor on the machine reports. The missing evidence is the local friction floor before braking begins. The stopping calculation below evaluates this unobserved friction deficit:

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-oil-film
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE OIL FILM ON THE AISLE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-frontier-epistemic-limits (the premise behind the aisle
# │          speed), @sec-frontier-residual-claims-register (the register
# │          entries and @tbl-17-claims-register),
# │          @sec-frontier-failures-without-detectors (detection latency against the spare margin),
# │          @sec-frontier-fallacies-pitfalls (the vision-only pitfall).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that the 1.3 m/s normal mode always rested on a friction
# │          floor that no sensor on the machine reports.
# │ Show:    the friction the credible deceleration needs; the stop on a clear
# │          film against the clear distance; the inspected-floor ceiling and
# │          restricted mode; the zero-failure closure test; the time the spare
# │          margin buys. The walking-person ceiling is Ch12's
# │          (@sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes) and is cited, not recomputed.
# │ How:     credible deceleration a = min(a_brake, mu g); the finished budget
# │          (C2 stop, all three overheads) at the aisle speed; its ceiling as
# │          the positive root with a_eff = a / 1.5; zero-failure sample size.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class OilFilm:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    g = (1 * ureg.standard_gravity).to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**2)  # category: measured (physical constant, standard gravity)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (credible deceleration, dry floor)
    mu_dry = AISLE.mu_dry  # category: illustrative (dry concrete)
    mu_insp = AISLE.mu_inspected_floor  # category: illustrative (inspected floor)
    mu_oil = AISLE.mu_oil_film  # category: illustrative (clear hydraulic film)
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen (normal-mode aisle speed)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end clear distance)
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (total pre-brake delay)
    overhead = AISLE.fixed_overhead  # category: derived (delta_loc + delta_margin + eps_track)
    v_h = AISLE.v_human_approach  # category: datasheet (ISO 13855 walking speed)
    v_restricted = 1.0 * ureg.meter / ureg.second  # category: chosen (scenario assumption: restricted mode on inspected floors)
    p_miss_target = 0.001  # category: chosen (detector miss-rate bound for closure)
    n_contrast = 1000  # category: illustrative (a smaller zero-miss campaign, for contrast)
    confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen (one-sided confidence level)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    mu_min = (a_brake / g).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    a_dry = min(a_brake, mu_dry * g)
    a_insp = min(a_brake, mu_insp * g)
    a_oil = min(a_brake, mu_oil * g)

    # finished budget at the aisle speed: v tau + 0.75 v^2/a (C2 stop) + overhead
    budget_aisle = (v_aisle * tau_delay + calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_aisle, a_dry)["distance"] + overhead).to(ureg.meter)
    spare_aisle = (d_clear - budget_aisle).to(ureg.millimeter)
    t_latest = (spare_aisle / v_aisle).to(ms)
    stop_oil = (v_aisle * tau_delay + calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_aisle, a_oil)["distance"] + overhead).to(ureg.meter)

    # ceilings: positive root of the finished budget with a_eff = a / 1.5
    margin_loc = AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.eps_track
    ceiling_dry = calc_max_permitted_velocity(d_clear, tau_delay, a_dry / 1.5, margin_loc, AISLE.delta_margin)
    ceiling_insp = calc_max_permitted_velocity(d_clear, tau_delay, a_insp / 1.5, margin_loc, AISLE.delta_margin)

    n_closure = calc_zero_failure_sample_size(1.0 - p_miss_target, confidence=confidence)
    p_miss_contrast = 1.0 - calc_clopper_pearson_zero_failure_bound(n_contrast, confidence=confidence)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(mu_min - 0.204) < 5e-4, f"Friction floor should be 0.204, got {mu_min}.")
    check(a_dry == a_brake and mu_dry > mu_min, "On dry concrete the brakes, not friction, must bind.")
    check(mu_oil < mu_min and mu_insp < mu_min, "On the film and on an inspected floor friction must bind.")
    check(abs(a_insp.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**2).magnitude - 1.1768) < 5e-4, f"Inspected-floor deceleration should be 1.18 m/s², got {a_insp}.")
    check(abs(budget_aisle.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 997.43) < 5e-3, f"Budget at 1.3 m/s should be 997.43 mm, got {budget_aisle}.")
    check(abs(spare_aisle.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 102.57) < 5e-3, f"Spare at 1.3 m/s should be 102.57 mm, got {spare_aisle}.")
    check(abs(t_latest.to(ms).magnitude - 78.9) < 5e-2, f"T_latest should be 78.9 ms, got {t_latest}.")
    check(abs(ceiling_dry.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 1.3898) < 5e-5, f"Dry-floor ceiling should be 1.3898 m/s, got {ceiling_dry}.")
    check(
        abs(ceiling_insp.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second).magnitude - 1.0947) < 5e-5, f"Inspected-floor ceiling should be 1.0947 m/s, got {ceiling_insp}."
    )
    check(
        v_restricted < ceiling_insp < v_aisle < ceiling_dry,
        "Restricted mode must sit under the inspected ceiling, and the aisle speed under the dry ceiling.",
    )
    check(abs(stop_oil.to(ureg.meter).magnitude - 2.95) < 5e-3, f"Finished budget on the film should be 2.95 m, got {stop_oil}.")
    check(abs(a_oil.to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**2).magnitude - 0.49) < 5e-3, f"Film deceleration should be 0.49 m/s², got {a_oil}.")
    check(stop_oil > 2 * d_clear, f"On the film the stop from the aisle speed must exceed twice the clear distance, got {stop_oil}.")
    check(n_closure == 2995, f"Zero-failure closure test should need 2,995 trials, got {n_closure}.")
    check(abs(p_miss_contrast - 0.002991) < 5e-7, f"1,000 zero-miss trials should bound the miss rate at 0.002991, got {p_miss_contrast}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, precision=0)
    mu_min_str = fmt(mu_min, precision=3)
    mu_dry_str = fmt(mu_dry, precision=2)
    mu_insp_str = fmt(mu_insp, precision=2)
    mu_oil_str = fmt(mu_oil, precision=2)
    a_insp_str = fmt_acceleration(a_insp, precision=2)
    a_oil_str = fmt_acceleration(a_oil, precision=2)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    budget_aisle_str = fmt_length(budget_aisle, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    spare_aisle_str = fmt_length(spare_aisle, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    t_latest_str = fmt_latency(t_latest, unit=ms, precision=1)
    stop_oil_str = fmt_length(stop_oil, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    ceiling_insp_str = fmt_velocity(ceiling_insp, precision=2)
    v_restricted_str = fmt_velocity(v_restricted, precision=0)
    n_closure_str = fmt_int(n_closure, commas=True)
    n_contrast_str = fmt_int(n_contrast, commas=True)
    p_miss_contrast_str = fmt(p_miss_contrast, precision=6)
    p_miss_target_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_miss_target, precision=1, style="prose")
    p_miss_target_sym_str = fmt_percent(p_miss_target, precision=1, style="symbol")
    confidence_pct_str = fmt_percent(confidence, precision=0, style="prose")
    confidence_sym_str = fmt_percent(confidence, precision=0, style="symbol")
    v_h_str = fmt_velocity(v_h, precision=1)
```

The release decision of @sec-release-safety-cases-claims already met this premise. Its claim C3, braking traction, was refused on the book's own evidence and handed to this chapter as an open premise. The machine's credible deceleration is the smaller of what its mechanical brakes deliver and what the floor interface supplies:
$$a = \min(a_{\text{brake}}, \mu g).$$
The `{python} OilFilm.a_brake_str` credible deceleration that @sec-body-kinetic-momentum established requires a physical friction coefficient of at least $\mu \ge$ `{python} OilFilm.mu_min_str`. Dry industrial concrete, at a measured $\mu$ of `{python} OilFilm.mu_dry_str`, supplies far more traction, so the mechanical brakes bind and govern deceleration. The clear hydraulic film, at $\mu$ = `{python} OilFilm.mu_oil_str` (both coefficients illustrative; see the Reader Guide), supplies only `{python} OilFilm.a_oil_str`, and the tire-floor interface binds. At the `{python} OilFilm.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, the finished budget of @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget, `{python} OilFilm.budget_aisle_str` on a dry floor, grows on the film to `{python} OilFilm.stop_oil_str` against a `{python} OilFilm.d_clear_str` clear distance.

This numerical explosion reveals the central insight of the epistemic frontier: the friction premise did not suddenly become open when the fluid leaked onto the concrete. The normal operating mode that @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes selected rested on that unmeasured friction floor on every aisle, the dry ones included, and no sensor on the machine had ever measured it.

This reality reinforces why Physical AI is fundamentally an architectural discipline rather than an end-to-end model optimization problem. In an end-to-end robotic policy, unmodeled physical variations—such as a transparent oil film, an uncalibrated force sensor, or an unobserved slip transition during high-dexterity manipulation—propagate unhindered from sensory inputs directly to motor currents. Dependable embodied architectures instead structurally decouple unprivileged statistical proposals from deterministic real-time enforcers across the complete Physical AI Systems stack:

1. **Silicon and Inverter Layer (20 kHz to 50 kHz)**: At the hardware foundation, Field-Oriented Control (FOC) inverters execute inner current loops on dedicated field-programmable gate array (FPGA) or digital signal processor (DSP) logic, utilizing Space Vector Modulation (SVM) and shunt current sensing to regulate motor torque ($\tau = \frac{3}{2} p \lambda_m i_q$) while enforcing hard Safe Torque Off (STO) relays and overcurrent trips.
2. **Deterministic Nervous System and Safety Shield (1 kHz)**: An isolated real-time processor executing an RTOS (such as RT-Linux or FreeRTOS) communicates deterministically over industrial buses (EtherCAT, CAN-FD, or TSN). This layer evaluates Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) and kinematic feasibility, treating learned commands strictly as unprivileged proposals and projecting them into certified safe sets or triggering physical braking fallbacks when invariants are breached.
3. **Spatial Perception and Dynamic Memory (30 Hz to 100 Hz)**: Synchronized sensor pipelines fuse multi-camera RGB-D streams, lidar point clouds, and high-resolution tactile matrices into SE(3) pose estimates, dynamic occupancy grids, and spatial representations.
4. **Foundation Action Model and High-Level Brain (5 Hz to 20 Hz)**: Large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models and diffusion action policies generate semantic task plans and multi-step action chunks, optimizing task completion within the sandboxed envelope maintained by the deterministic layers below.

Every engineering method has a physical boundary where its guarantees expire. The physical wall of @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws is one such boundary, because scaling up a learned foundation model cannot reduce the travel that its own computational latency and inference delay cost the machine. Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety [@ashby1956introduction] formalizes another: a controller cannot regulate disturbances that its sensory architecture cannot perceive. On the mobile manipulator, the transparent oil film is an unobserved disturbance.

The manipulator arm's contact limit at the door latch rests on a premise of the identical kind: a structural latch that holds at every force below the arm's contact ceiling. Yet mechanical wear, material fatigue, or chemical corrosion can silently lower the latch's yield force below that ceiling while the joint torque sensors read exactly what they would read against a sound latch. Similarly, a wrist force-torque sensor that limits manipulation contact forces below a fragile workpiece threshold depends on an unshifted analog calibration. Mechanical shock, adhesive creep, or strain gauge thermal drift can shift that zero reference until the control loop regulates against a phantom reading while the true contact wrench breaches structural yield.

In each case, the machine departs from its certified operating conditions while its internal telemetry remains completely nominal. Successful empirical trials cannot close such a gap: the exposure wall that @sec-evaluation-trial-limits derives places a rare-hazard rate beyond any practical failure-free test campaign. The safety case must explicitly name the missing premise, restrict operational authority while it remains open, and state what empirical evidence could close it. For each open premise, systems discipline asks what the machine can physically measure, what its actuators can still prevent, and which operational claims must remain refused.

## Theoretical Boundaries and Unprovable Invariants {#sec-frontier-method-limits}

The mobile manipulator's release claim is a chain of dependent links determined by the operational hazards and the selected mitigations (@sec-boundary-machine-model). The argument must establish the operating domain, measured actuator and stopping bounds, component contracts, and independent permission for learned proposals. Hazards controlled by runtime detection also need measured detector coverage and timely monitoring. Hazards controlled by passive limits or operating restrictions instead need evidence that those measures hold over the declared load, wear, and exposure envelope. Generating extensive evidence for one link cannot compensate for an unsupported premise in another.[^fn-hist-popper-falsification]

[^fn-hist-popper-falsification]: **Popperian Falsification**\index{Falsification!Popperian induction}: Karl Popper formalized the asymmetry of empirical induction: no finite sequence of safe observations can prove universal safety, whereas a single counterexample refutes it. Operational fleet hours establish survival rates strictly under observed stationary conditions, not out-of-distribution guarantees. Extrapolating zero observed incidents to unbounded environments produces an illusory sense of safety that fails upon encountering unmodeled edge cases.

Each premise of a safety case carries one of the Reader Guide's five statuses (established by measurement or derivation, assumed, decided by accountable judgment, unsupported, or outside the threat model). The envelope trichotomy (\ref{dfn-release-envelope-trichotomy}) places a premise that a runtime monitor checks as known-true, known-false, or unknown. The premises that bound the evidence here are ones no monitor now in service can check, so none can become known-true, and the release, not the monitor, must restrict operation around them. For the base, the stopping-distance claim relies on an assumed friction coefficient between wheel and floor that cannot be measured before braking begins. For the arm, the contact argument depends on a declared floor on the strength of the latch and the objects it handles, a floor decided by engineering judgment about structural yield, while the latch's present strength stays unmeasured between proof tests. For the wrist transducer, the force-limit claim assumes a sensor whose zero point has not drifted, a premise that its own live telemetry cannot check without an unloaded physical tare. Naming these premises explicitly does not weaken the release record. It establishes the physical envelope within which the release verdict is justified, and outside of which the verdict ceases to apply.

Separating measurement from judgment is fundamental to systems engineering discipline. Empirical testing and statistical characterization can estimate physical exposure, quantify sensor noise, and bound parametric uncertainty, but no measurement can choose an acceptable **residual risk**\index{Residual risk} or decide which individuals in an operational environment must bear that risk. Those choices are accountable human decisions that must be recorded as explicit judgments rather than disguised as empirical findings. In the same way, the **threat model**\index{Threat model} bounds the validity of the record. Empirical testing across nominal fleet operations and accidental component faults provides no evidence regarding intentional adversarial attacks. A safety record demonstrating that a vision pipeline handles sensor noise, lens blur, and partial occlusions provides no statistical support for claims about resilience against adversarial optical projection, model parameter tampering, or intentional denial of service across the internal communication bus.

### Conditional shield dilution and common-cause bounds {#sec-frontier-shield-dilution}

When a learned policy operates under a real-time safety shield, systems designers frequently assume that the shield's mathematical guarantees eliminate the need to bound the failure rate of the underlying proposal model. This assumption fails under rigorous probabilistic accounting. The safety shield is a conditional filter whose effectiveness depends strictly on the proposal rate, interception coverage, and unshielded hardware failure terms, as modeled in the simulation below:

```{python}
#| label: calc-frontier-architectural-shield-dilution
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_sci, fmt, check
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_empirical_testing_exposure,
    calc_shielded_system_hazard_rate,
)

# ┌── 1. INPUT (Illustrative target and distinct evidence records) ────
p_target = 1.0e-9  # category: illustrative (system incidents/hour target, not a statutory rate)
confidence = 0.95  # category: chosen (one-sided confidence level)
alpha = 1.0 - confidence  # category: derived (significance level)

fleet_units = 100  # category: illustrative (fleet size)
t_cycle_days = 90.0  # category: illustrative (release cycle length)
hours_per_day = 24.0  # category: illustrative (continuous operation)

c_shield_assumed = 0.9999  # category: illustrative (class-specific interception coverage)
p_hw_assumed = 0.0  # category: illustrative (hardware and common-cause residual set to zero)
proposal_events_hypothetical = 0  # category: illustrative (adjudicated counterfactual-oracle proposal log)

# ┌── 2. COMPUTE (Proposal-log bound and shield decomposition) ────────
# The adjudicated proposal log covers one full cycle of the fleet.
t_cycle_hours = t_cycle_days * hours_per_day
proposal_exposure_hours_hypothetical = fleet_units * t_cycle_hours
# Zero hazardous proposals bound the proposal rate (one-sided Poisson).
p_proposal_upper_hypothetical = -math.log(alpha) / proposal_exposure_hours_hypothetical

# Conditional design arithmetic: the proposal-rate bound the target would require
# at the assumed class-specific interception coverage, and the exposure to show it.
p_proposal_limit = (p_target - p_hw_assumed) / (1.0 - c_shield_assumed)
n_brain_hours = calc_empirical_testing_exposure(p_proposal_limit, confidence=confidence)
t_test_days = n_brain_hours.magnitude / (fleet_units * hours_per_day)
p_system_conditional = calc_shielded_system_hazard_rate(
    p_proposal_upper_hypothetical / ureg.hour, c_shield_assumed, p_hw_assumed / ureg.hour
).magnitude
c_required_cycle = 1.0 - (p_target - p_hw_assumed) / p_proposal_upper_hypothetical
test_overrun_days = t_test_days - t_cycle_days

# ┌── 3. GUARDS (Statistical bounds & invariance checks) ──────────────
check(abs(proposal_exposure_hours_hypothetical - 216000.0) < 1.0, f"Unexpected proposal-log hours: {proposal_exposure_hours_hypothetical}")
check(abs(p_proposal_upper_hypothetical - 1.3869e-5) < 1e-8, f"Unexpected proposal bound: {p_proposal_upper_hypothetical}")
check(proposal_events_hypothetical == 0, "Proposal scenario requires zero events")
check(abs(p_proposal_limit - 1.0e-5) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected proposal limit: {p_proposal_limit}")
check(abs(n_brain_hours.magnitude - 299573.0) < 100.0, f"Unexpected brain exposure: {n_brain_hours}")
check(abs(t_test_days - 124.8) < 1.0, f"Unexpected test days: {t_test_days}")
check(abs(p_system_conditional - 1.386913e-9) < 1e-12, f"Unexpected conditional residual: {p_system_conditional}")
check(abs(c_required_cycle - 0.9999278974) < 1e-8, f"Unexpected required coverage: {c_required_cycle}")
check(test_overrun_days > 34.0, f"Unexpected 90-day overrun: {test_overrun_days}")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Canonical formatting) ────────────────────────────────
class ArchitecturalShieldDilution:
    n_proposal_sci_str = fmt_sci(proposal_exposure_hours_hypothetical, precision=2)
    p_proposal_upper_sci_str = fmt_sci(p_proposal_upper_hypothetical, precision=3)

    p_brain_sci_str = fmt_sci(p_proposal_limit, precision=0)
    n_brain_sci_str = fmt_sci(n_brain_hours.magnitude, precision=2)
    t_test_days_str = fmt(t_test_days, precision=3)
    p_system_conditional_sci_str = fmt_sci(p_system_conditional, precision=3)
    c_required_str = fmt(c_required_cycle, precision=7)
    test_overrun_days_str = fmt(test_overrun_days, precision=1)
```

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The empirical exposure wall and minimal-intervention safety shields are established in @sec-evaluation and @sec-enforcement.
:::

Take as the system target an illustrative $10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}$, a rate that no standard assigns to this machine and that, by the exposure wall, operating hours alone cannot demonstrate.[^fn-math-exposure-updates] The remaining question is what the permission path can add to the claim when it acts between proposal and actuation as the safety shield, and which of its premises need evidence of their own.

[^fn-math-exposure-updates]: **Evidence Across Updates**\index{Exposure wall!retraining reset}: An updated model may alter the proposal distribution. Earlier data can be pooled only with a justified configuration-equivalence and exposure argument; an update does not automatically erase every observation. The exposure wall's constant-rate model also requires a defensible treatment of shared fleet conditions and correlated faults.

A shield argument is *conditional*, not a multiplication applied to observed system incidents. A pervasive fallacy among machine learning teams is to take the observed system incident rate $\lambda_{\mathrm{system}}$ from historical fleet logs and multiply it by $(1 - c_h)$, claiming that introducing a safety shield reduces risk by that factor. In reality, observed fleet incidents already reflect the residual failure rate *after* existing mitigations or operator overrides have acted. Multiplying observed incident counts by $(1 - c_h)$ erroneously squares the shield's credit, inventing four orders of magnitude of phantom reliability! For a defined hazard class $h$, let $\lambda_{\mathrm{proposal},h}$ be the arrival rate of raw, unshielded hazardous proposed actions emitted by the neural policy before the permission layer, and let $c_h=P(\mathrm{intercept}\mid\mathrm{hazardous\ proposal},h)$ be measured interception coverage for that specific class. With a separately bounded hardware and common-cause term $\lambda_{\mathrm{other}}$, the true conditional hazard rate is governed by @eq-frontier-shielded-hazard:
$$\lambda_{\mathrm{system},h} \le \lambda_{\mathrm{proposal},h}(1-c_h)+\lambda_{\mathrm{other}}$$ {#eq-frontier-shielded-hazard}
The relation requires a valid proposal oracle, timely detection, actuator authority, and a justified treatment of correlated failures. It gives no credit for an oil film or a weakened latch that the shield cannot observe, and no release follows from the arithmetic until each premise is supported.

Evaluating this conditional hazard decomposition requires bounding the unshielded proposal arrival rate $\lambda_{\mathrm{proposal},h}$ from empirical telemetry logs before applying shield credit. Under a stationary Poisson model with zero observed hazardous proposals, this bound is governed by the Rule of Three (@sec-verification, @eq-verification-rule-of-three):

::: {#nbk-frontier-fleet-exposure-and-shielded-decomposition .callout-notebook title="A conditional shield calculation"}

**Problem**: One hundred robots keep a fully adjudicated proposal log for one 90-day cycle, judged by a validated counterfactual oracle, and the log records no hazardous proposal. If a named shield's interception coverage for that hazard class were independently established at $c=0.9999$, would the modeled residual meet the $10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}$ system target?

**Proposal bound**: Under a stationary Poisson model, zero hazardous proposals in `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.n_proposal_sci_str` proposal-hours give a one-sided 95 percent upper bound of `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_proposal_upper_sci_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$.

**Residual**: With hardware and common-cause residual set to zero for this calculation, @eq-frontier-shielded-hazard gives `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_system_conditional_sci_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$, **above** the target. The coverage the target requires is at least `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.c_required_str`.

**Required proposal evidence**: At $c=0.9999$ the proposal-rate bound must fall to `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.p_brain_sci_str` $\text{h}^{-1}$. Zero adjudicated hazardous proposals would then require `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.n_brain_sci_str` proposal-hours, or `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.t_test_days_str` days for 100 units, `{python} ArchitecturalShieldDilution.test_overrun_days_str` days beyond the cycle.

**Systems insight**: A shield changes the system claim only for hazard classes it can detect and intercept in time. Proposal frequency, conditional interception coverage, hardware faults, and common-cause failures need separate evidence. Oil or material failure outside the shield's sensing coverage stays in the residual-claims register.
:::

To prevent unwarranted reliance on safety shields, systems engineers must enforce **the three preconditions of barrier validity**:

1. **Full state observability, directional tangent validity, and non-smooth contact mechanics**: A barrier certificate $h(x) \ge 0$ is valid if and only if the physical state $x(t)$ is observable from sensor telemetry $y(t)$ and the affine dynamic model $\dot{x} = f(x) + g(x)u$ matches physical reality. In control literature, the classical notation of the **Lie derivative** ($L_f h(x)$) frequently obscures a familiar multivariable calculus operation: it is simply the directional derivative of the scalar safety margin $h(x)$ along the vector field of unforced physical dynamics $f(x)$, computed directly via the multivariable chain rule:
   $$L_f h(x) \equiv \nabla h(x) \cdot f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^d \frac{\partial h}{\partial x_i} f_i(x).$$
   For an ML systems engineer accustomed to gradient computations and Jacobian-vector products, $\nabla h(x) \cdot f(x)$ answers a concrete physical question: *If all actuators are de-energized, at what rate does passive Newtonian inertia expand or shrink the safety margin?* If $\nabla h(x) \cdot f(x) < 0$, unforced physics is actively consuming safety clearance. Similarly, the control Lie derivative $L_g h(x) \equiv \nabla h(x) \cdot g(x)$ measures the directional sensitivity of the safety margin to commanded actuator inputs $u$. A Control Barrier Function enforces forward invariance by requiring the total time derivative $\dot{h}(x, u)$ to satisfy:
   $$\dot{h}(x, u) = \nabla h(x) \cdot f(x) + (\nabla h(x) \cdot g(x)) u \ge -\alpha(h(x))$$
   where $\alpha(\cdot)$ is an extended class-$\mathcal{K}$ comparison function bounding how rapidly the system may safely approach the boundary. If tire friction $\mu$ drops, sensor latency $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ stretches, or payload inertia shifts without being observed, the true physical vector field $f_{\text{true}}(x)$ departs from the model $f(x)$. The directional derivative $\nabla h(x) \cdot f(x)$ evaluates along an erroneous tangent: the quadratic program believes it is preserving forward invariance, while along the true physical trajectory $\nabla h(x) \cdot f_{\text{true}}(x)$ has collapsed, projecting the machine directly across the safety boundary.

   Furthermore, standard Control Barrier Functions assume continuously differentiable vector fields ($f \in C^1$) and smooth trajectories. In physical robotics, however, foundational contact mechanics is governed by non-smooth **Signorini complementarity conditions** and Coulomb friction cones:
   $$0 \le \phi(q) \perp \lambda_N \ge 0, \quad \lambda_N \cdot \phi(q) = 0$$
   where $\phi(q)$ is the signed distance (gap function) between contacting bodies and $\lambda_N$ is the normal contact force. At the exact instant of physical impact—such as a foot strike during whole-body dynamic locomotion, or finger-object impact during high-dexterity tactile manipulation—the velocity vector field experiences an impulsive jump discontinuity governed by the Newton-Euler impact equation:
   $$M(q) (\dot{q}^+ - \dot{q}^-) = J_c(q)^T \Lambda$$
   where $\Lambda$ is the contact impulse and $J_c(q)$ is the contact Jacobian. At that impact instant, acceleration approaches infinity (a Dirac delta distribution), rendering the smooth Lie derivative $\nabla h(x) \cdot f(x)$ mathematically undefined. If the safety filter does not explicitly model hybrid contact phase transitions and non-smooth barrier certificates, forward invariance collapses precisely when the physical impact occurs.
2. **Actuator authority and inverter feasibility margins**: The quadratic program (QP) that filters unprivileged control proposals into certified commands:
   $$u^* = \operatorname{argmin}_{u \in \mathcal{U}} \|u - u_{\text{learned}}\|^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \nabla h(x) \cdot f(x) + (\nabla h(x) \cdot g(x)) u \ge -\alpha(h(x))$$
   assumes that the admissible control set $\mathcal{U}$ is non-empty. On physical hardware, actuator authority is bounded not merely by kinematic velocity limits, but by the electrical and thermal constraints of the Field-Oriented Control (FOC) inverter. In permanent magnet synchronous motors, delivered torque follows $\tau = \frac{3}{2} p \lambda_m i_q$, where quadrature current $i_q$ is bounded by DC bus voltage $V_{\text{dc}}$ and rotor back-EMF ($V_{\text{emf}} = p \lambda_m \omega$). At high rotational velocities, back-EMF shrinks voltage headroom, causing available torque to decay nonlinearly: $\tau_{\max}(\omega) \le \frac{3}{2} p \lambda_m \frac{V_{\text{dc}} - p \lambda_m \omega}{R}$. If an unprivileged policy drives the machine into a high-momentum state where the deceleration required to satisfy $\dot{h} \ge -\alpha(h)$ exceeds physical braking capacity ($a_{\text{req}} > \min(a_{\text{brake}}, \mu g)$) or dynamic inverter limits, the constraint set becomes empty, the QP solver returns `INFEASIBLE`, and the barrier certificate collapses.
3. **Independent hardware fault paths and Safe Torque Off**: A software safety shield executing on the same host operating system or system-on-chip as the proposal model shares common-cause failure modes, including memory corruption, kernel panics, and voltage brownouts. A mathematically verified barrier provides zero protection unless backed by independent physical hardware cutoffs—such as electromechanical Safe Torque Off (STO) relays and hardware watchdogs that de-energize gate drivers within milliseconds when communication or heartbeats fail.

### The empirical exposure wall and the rule of three {#sec-frontier-empirical-exposure-wall}

Under a stationary Poisson model, observing zero failure events over cumulative exposure time $T$ yields the foundational **Rule of Three** established in @sec-verification (@eq-verification-rule-of-three): demonstrating that a target failure rate does not exceed $\lambda$ at 95 percent confidence requires accumulating at least $T \ge 3.0 / \lambda$ continuous zero-failure operating hours ($4.61 / \lambda$ at 99 percent confidence).

This mathematical relationship creates the unyielding **Poisson Exposure Wall**\index{Exposure wall!Poisson bounds}. To certify an ultra-dependable industrial or aviation target rate of $\lambda = 10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}$ (1 Failure in Time, or FIT), empirical testing requires accumulating at least:
$$T \ge \frac{3.0}{10^{-9}\text{ h}^{-1}} = 3 \times 10^9\text{ hours}$$
of continuous, failure-free operation. That exposure corresponds to over $342{,}000$ vehicle-years of continuous operation. Even a massive commercial fleet of $1{,}000$ autonomous robots operating 24 hours a day, 365 days a year accumulates only $8.76 \times 10^6$ fleet hours annually, requiring more than $340$ calendar years to demonstrate that target empirically.

The exposure wall is equally unyielding in autonomous driving, where human fatality rates average approximately one death per $100$ million miles ($10^{-8}$ fatalities per mile). Under classical statistical bounds, demonstrating with 95 percent confidence that an autonomous fleet matches human safety requires accumulating roughly $275$ million failure-free miles; establishing statistical rate precision requires more than $8.8$ billion miles [@kalra2016driving]. For an autonomous fleet of $100$ vehicles driving continuously at $30\text{ mph}$, collecting $8.8$ billion miles requires over $330$ calendar years. Gathering more nominal operational data cannot breach this barrier; rare catastrophic hazards inhabit the unobserved tail of physical reality.

### The curse of dimensionality and formal verification ceilings {#sec-frontier-verification-ceilings}

When empirical fleet exposure fails to breach the astronomical exposure wall, system safety cannot be rescued simply by retreating into offline mathematical proof (@fig-17-state-space-formal-verification-frontier). Formal safety verification confronts an equally unyielding epistemic limit: the **curse of dimensionality** across continuous state spaces.

In formal verification, **reachability analysis**\index{Reachability analysis!Hamilton-Jacobi PDE} computes all physical states from which worst-case disturbances force the system into an unsafe set (the *backward reachable tube*). For machine learning systems engineers familiar with reinforcement learning and value iteration, classical Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability is best understood as **continuous-state, continuous-time minimax Bellman dynamic programming** evaluated backward in time:
$$\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + \min_{u \in \mathcal{U}} \max_{d \in \mathcal{D}} \left( \nabla V(x, t) \cdot f(x, u, d) \right) = 0$$
In this formulation, nature acts as an adversarial agent choosing disturbance $d \in \mathcal{D}$ (aerodynamic wind gusts, friction drops, communication latency) to minimize the safety value function $V(x, t)$, while defensive control inputs $u \in \mathcal{U}$ seek to maximize it. The zero-level set of $V(x, t)$ isolates the exact boundary where defensive control can no longer prevent an impending collision. To solve this differential game numerically, the continuous state space $\mathcal{X} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ must be discretized into a spatial grid.

Here lies the impenetrable **Grid Wall**\index{Grid Wall!exponential state-space complexity}: if each state dimension is discretized into a modest resolution of $N = 100$ grid points, computing the PDE requires evaluating $N^d = 100^d = 10^{2d}$ grid cells:

- **3D Dubins Car** ($x, y, \theta$): $d = 3 \implies 100^3 = 10^6$ cells (one million points, requiring roughly $8\text{ MB}$ of memory and easily solved in seconds on a workstation).
- **6D Planar Biped or Kinematic Vehicle** ($x, y, \theta, v, \dot{\theta}, a$): $d = 6 \implies 100^6 = 10^{12}$ cells (one trillion points, requiring $8\text{ TB}$ of memory and cluster-scale compute).
- **12D Quadrotor** (3D position, 3D velocity, 3D orientation, 3D rates): $d = 12 \implies 100^{12} = 10^{24}$ cells, requiring $8 \times 10^{24}$ bytes of memory for double-precision grid values—vastly exceeding the entire global manufacturing supply of silicon DRAM.
- **High-Dexterity Tactile Hand or Mobile Manipulator** ($d = 30\text{ to }48$): A multi-fingered hand grasping a deformable object or an articulated base with dual arms spans joint positions, velocities, and contact states, yielding $100^{30} = 10^{60}$ to $100^{48} = 10^{96}$ cells, placing grid evaluation beyond the number of atoms in the observable universe.
- **Non-Rigid Deformable Objects**: Manipulating cables, cloth, elastomeric seals, or soft tissue involves infinite-dimensional configuration spaces ($\mathcal{C} = \mathbb{R}^\infty$). Finite element approximations with hundreds of nodes ($d > 500$) render grid-based reachability mathematically impossible.

Consequently, exact grid-based reachability analysis hits an unyielding dimensional ceiling at $d \approx 6$. Sampling-based statistical verification (such as adaptive stress testing and scenario optimization) breaks the exponential grid wall, scaling polynomially as $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ up to 50 dimensions or more; yet it purchases tractability by surrendering deterministic safety guarantees, yielding only probabilistic Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) bounds ($1 - \epsilon$) that remain inherently blind to measure-zero adversarial singularities. Modern neural barrier certificates (NBCs) synthesized via branch-and-bound verification tools (such as $\alpha,\beta$-CROWN) establish a promising intermediate frontier, verifying forward invariance across 12D to 30D robotic systems through convex relaxations and Linear Relaxation Perturbation Analysis (LiRPA, $\mathcal{O}(d^k)$). Even so, when state dimensionality scales to coupled multi-robot swarms ($d \ge 48$), verification times again escalate toward intractability, demonstrating that formal methods replace exposure time with state-space dimensional ceilings rather than eliminating epistemic limits.

::: {#fig-17-state-space-formal-verification-frontier fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The formal verification tractability frontier across state-space dimensionality**: Computation time (seconds, log scale) required to synthesize or verify safe control invariants as a function of continuous state-space dimension $d$. Hamilton-Jacobi reachability (red) provides deterministic continuous guarantees via grid-based partial differential equations ($\\mathcal{O}(N^d)$), hitting the exponential Grid Wall at $d > 6$. Sampling-based statistical verification (green dashed, $\\mathcal{O}(d^2)$) scales polynomially to high dimensions but provides only probabilistic PAC bounds ($1 - \\epsilon$), blind to measure-zero corner failures. Neural barrier certificates verified via branch-and-bound SMT solvers ($\\alpha,\\beta$-CROWN, dark blue, $\\mathcal{O}(d^k)$) push the formal frontier across 12D quadrotors, 16D bipedal robots, and 30D mobile manipulators before computational scaling limits coupled multi-agent swarms ($d \\ge 48$)." fig-alt="Log-linear chart showing verification computation time from milliseconds to centuries across state-space dimensionality from 2 to 50. Hamilton-Jacobi reachability shoots upward exponentially, hitting the Grid Wall at dimension 6. Sampling-based verification scales polynomially as a gentle slope. Neural barrier certificates scale moderately through 12D quadrotor, 16D biped, and 30D mobile manipulator benchmarks, showing how modern relaxations push the formal verification frontier."}


Each of these premises, from friction under a film to a shield's coverage for a hazard class it may not observe, ends the same way, named by the release and left unsettled by its evidence. A release that stops at naming them has only listed its caveats. What it needs is a record that turns each such premise into a restriction with an owner and a test that can end it.

## A Residual-Claims Register {#sec-frontier-residual-claims-register}

Refusing claim C3 did not remove the friction premise from the machine, and an unproven premise remains whether or not a safety report records it. The **residual-claims register**\index{Residual-claims register!definition} represents the sixteenth and culminating contract of this book. Emitted as the ultimate governance artifact of the Physical AI stack, it consumes the upstream release manifest of @sec-release-manifest, capturing every premise the release left open or unsupported. In disembodied software engineering, unresolved bugs and architectural shortcuts linger as non-blocking technical debt in an issue tracker while new model weights are continuously pushed to production. If an unhandled exception or memory leak occurs in a web service, the container orchestrator restarts the pod, logs an HTTP 500 error, or redirects traffic to a replica. In Physical AI, however, epistemic debt is kinetic debt. An unverified physical premise is not an abstract software flaw; it is unbraked momentum, uncontrolled mechanical force, or high-voltage energy committed across a continuous causal boundary. If an autonomous machine ships with an unmeasured friction floor or an uncalibrated force sensor, that debt is amortized in physical impact. When the unmodeled condition manifests, the failure terminates in plastic deformation or human trauma governed by the conservation laws of motion. The residual-claims register mathematically binds autonomous authority to empirical evidence: an open entry enforces an active, machine-readable restriction that derates operational authority until its predeclared closure test passes.

The register maps each such premise, and every unmonitored invariant, to four mandatory components: its missing physical observable, its active containment or operating restriction, an accountable human owner, and a predeclared empirical closure test. Without these four components, an unresolved premise is an unwritten risk, not an engineering contract. The register is where principle \ref{pri-vol4-evidence-bounds-authority} reaches the premises that evidence could not settle, holding machine authority to a safe restriction wherever supporting evidence is absent.

::: {#dfn-frontier-residual-claims-register .callout-definition title="Residual-claims register"}

***Residual-claims register***\index{Residual-claims register!definition}\index{Contracts!residual claims} is the sixteenth executable contract of the Physical AI stack, consuming the safety case release manifest to record every open or unsupported physical premise and mapping each to its missing physical observable, active operating restriction, accountable human owner, and predeclared empirical closure test.

1.  **Significance**: Prevents unsupported physical premises from vanishing into uncalibrated software optimism, mathematically holding autonomous machine authority to a restricted operational envelope until empirical or physical evidence proves safe boundaries.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a static hazard log or bug tracker, the residual-claims register is an active, machine-readable deployment contract integrated into firmware flashing and continuous deployment (CD) pipelines, enforcing operational deratings at runtime.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating open safety premises as speculative engineering debt to be resolved in future releases without derating operational speed or restricting the physical operating domain today.

:::

Each entry links the unsupported claim to the specific unmeasurable physical observable. In a machine that moves mass, a learned policy fails to settle a safety property because sensors cannot transduce the relevant environmental state, the computing substrate cannot process the measurement within the control deadline, or the physical interaction cannot be observed before contact occurs. An engineer must define the **missing observable**\index{Missing observable!definition} with physical precision rather than statistical abstractions. Characterizing an unknown failure as an "out-of-distribution latent state" provides no actionable signal for the permission loop to trigger a physical intervention. By contrast, stating an unmeasured surface friction coefficient, an undetected optical flare across a camera lens array, an unobservable micro-fracture in an actuator housing, or an unmodeled shear stress distribution across a tactile fingertip identifies the exact physical deficit. Naming the missing observable establishes the boundary where learned inference stops and physical uncertainty begins.

In high-dexterity manipulation of non-rigid deformable objects—such as routing flexible wire harnesses, manipulating elastomeric seals, or folding layered textiles—missing observables dominate the physical interaction. Surface RGB-D cameras observe only outer boundary geometry; they cannot transduce internal torsional strain, plastic deformation thresholds, or hidden entanglement states. When a gripper grasps an elastomeric gasket, the internal stress field is theoretically infinite-dimensional. If the foundation model's proposed trajectory induces shear forces exceeding the material's tear threshold, catastrophic failure occurs without any preceding visual anomaly. In the claims register, this gap cannot be resolved by gathering more nominal grasping demonstrations; it requires an active containment measure (such as a hardware torque-sensing compliant wrist or a tactile slip-monitoring reflex) and an explicit closure test (such as multi-axis force-torque proof testing across worst-case material batches).

The oil film gives the mobile manipulator its first entry. The premise is that every aisle floor supplies a friction coefficient of at least `{python} OilFilm.mu_min_str`, the value its credible deceleration needs. The missing observable is the friction beneath a clear film, which the navigation camera and the lidar cannot tell from dry concrete. The stop from the aisle speed that fits the clear distance on a dry floor overruns it on the film, so a speed limit the entry imposes can hold only on floors whose friction is measured or controlled.

An open entry requires an **operational response**\index{Operational response!definition}. For the aisles, the most the entry permits is a restricted mode of `{python} OilFilm.v_restricted_str` on floors under the site's inspection regime. An inspected floor supports $\mu \ge$ `{python} OilFilm.mu_insp_str`, which gives a credible deceleration of `{python} OilFilm.a_insp_str` and a ceiling of `{python} OilFilm.ceiling_insp_str`, so the restricted mode sits below its ceiling.[^fn-math-velocity-clamp] A route that the inspection regime does not cover is excluded, or the machine is withheld from it.

[^fn-math-velocity-clamp]: **Velocity Kinetic Derating**\index{Velocity clamp!kinetic derating}: $E_k=mv^2/2$ decreases quadratically with speed. Stopping distance still depends on a validated credible deceleration and total response delay; a speed register alone cannot compensate for arbitrarily low friction.

The restricted mode needs an owner able to keep its physical premises true. Site operations owns this entry through its spill procedure for pallet-jack routes, which sets the inspection interval and names the condition that withdraws permission. The signed speed limit on the permission path enforces the restriction, but a claim about friction cannot be maintained by a speed setting alone.

Every entry needs a **closure test**\index{Closure test!definition} declared before collecting data. For the film, the test must qualify a new transducer, because no measurement by the camera or the lidar can exclude a clear film and more trials with them could not close the entry. The test is a floor-film detector whose miss rate is bounded at `{python} OilFilm.p_miss_target_pct_str` by `{python} OilFilm.n_closure_str` failure-free trials on seeded films (@sec-evaluation-trial-limits); until it passes, the restriction holds. A smaller campaign falls short. Zero misses in `{python} OilFilm.n_contrast_str` independent trials bound the miss probability only at `{python} OilFilm.p_miss_contrast_str` with `{python} OilFilm.confidence_pct_str` confidence. The detector must also report the film early enough that detection, permission, and braking together fit the clear distance, and the trial distribution, detection distance, latency, false alarms, and friction after detection must be declared in advance. A wheel-slip reflex can limit later motion but cannot establish friction before the wheels reach the film.

The same aisle carries a second entry. The stopping budget protects a static obstacle. A person who keeps walking toward the machine through the whole stop adds distance that the budget never charges (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion), and @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes found that charging it would cap the base at this rack end far below its aisle speed. The premise is that no person approaches the rack end during a stop, and the missing observable is presence in the cross aisle the rack hides. The site's crossing rule, a floor-marked crossing plus a rack-end presence sensor, is the restriction, and site operations owns it. The closure test qualifies the presence sensor by the same zero-failure sizing.

The pick station adds a third entry, and this one belongs to the arm. Its premise is that the object the arm grasps, and later hands to the coworker under `accept_item` (@sec-intervention-human-authority), is the object the task names. @Sec-intent-request-to-proposal showed how that premise fails. A thin-walled red glass jar beside the red mug on the takeaway conveyor draws a confident grounding, and the wrong target passes every geometric check the planner and the permission path apply. The missing observable is identity and fragility, which neither the wrist camera nor the grounding model can establish before contact.

The restriction on this entry has two parts. Site operations admits to the conveyor only items on the pick station's declared item list, which holds no fragile look-alike, and the station admits a grasp only when the pick window holds exactly one object, so that a second object refuses the intent and sends the item to the coworker for a manual pick. Singulation makes the grounding unambiguous for the items it admits but supplies no identity information, and a mis-routed jar that arrives alone is contained only by the feed procedure. That residual is why the entry stays open. A grip-force ceiling set for the most fragile look-alike would need a crush limit for every item that might arrive, itself an unmeasured premise, so the register does not rest on one. Site operations owns the feed list and the singulation rule jointly with the task profile. The closure test is a qualified identity check at the station, a tag read or a scale-and-code check, whose false-accept rate is bounded at `{python} OilFilm.p_miss_target_pct_str` with `{python} OilFilm.confidence_pct_str` confidence by the same `{python} OilFilm.n_closure_str` failure-free trials, run here on seeded look-alikes.

@Tbl-17-claims-register sets the three entries side by side. Each row carries the four components the register requires, so any entry can be audited without the prose around it.
