For each, the register names the missing physical observable, the hazard it permits, the operating restriction and its accountable owner, and the predeclared closure test that would retire the restriction. {#tbl-17-claims-register tbl-colwidths="[22,24,26,28]"}

A release pipeline records each entry in a fixed schema, and its fields, units, and invariants appear with the other record layouts in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-residual-claims.

### Operationalizing open premises into engineering contracts {#sec-frontier-operationalizing-claims}

The residual-claims register is not a static archival report that engineers sign and shelf upon deployment. In dependable physical AI, the register functions as an executable software and operational contract integrated directly into continuous deployment (CD) and fleet telemetry pipelines.

When an engineering team pushes an updated model checkpoint or firmware configuration, the automated deployment pipeline validates the release against the wire schema of @sec-appendix-systems-wire-residual-claims. The target hardware's secure bootloader and isolated safety microcontroller parse the signed manifest directly from non-volatile storage. If an open premise lacks an empirical regression proof or if fleet telemetry reveals that physical conditions have departed from declared bounds (such as uninspected floor routes), the pipeline automatically flashes firmware enforcing the signed velocity clamp ($v \le 1.0\text{ m/s}$) and triggers operational alerts. The safety MCU physically refuses to arm high-speed actuation profiles ($1.3\text{ m/s}$) whenever the register contains an open claim lacking a cryptographically signed closure test artifact.

The physical execution architecture enforces this boundary across isolated silicon. The safety microcontroller (running a certified real-time operating system with deterministic 1 kHz cycle times) continuously monitors the active claims register. When an open claim imposes a restriction—such as a velocity clamp ($v \le 1.0\text{ m/s}$) or a contact force ceiling ($F \le 40\text{ N}$)—the safety MCU configures the motor inverter's digital signal processor (DSP) or FPGA via deterministic SPI or CAN-FD. The inverter's Field-Oriented Control (FOC) current loop, executing at 20 kHz to 50 kHz, clamps the quadrature-axis current limit ($i_q \le i_{q,\text{clamp}}$) and sets hardware comparator trip thresholds. If an unprivileged neural policy running on the host GPU attempts to emit commands violating these boundaries, the FOC inverter limits torque at the silicon level. If the host GPU hangs, suffers a memory fault, or fails to publish fresh heartbeat tokens within a hardware watchdog window ($t_{\text{watchdog}} \le 10\text{ ms}$), the safety MCU asserts Safe Torque Off (STO), opening electromechanical power relays to de-energize motor windings and engaging physical spring-set friction brakes. Physical containment does not trust the software stability of the proposal engine; it relies on silicon-level determinism.

All three entries close only through a qualified physical detector: a floor-film detector for the first, a rack-end presence sensor for the second, and an identity check at the station for the third. Each closure test must demonstrate that the qualified detector reports within strict real-time deadlines, ensuring that observation, permission arbitration, and braking fit within the available physical clearance. That timing requirement has a physical limit of its own.

## Failures Without Detectors {#sec-frontier-failures-without-detectors}

A runtime detector is itself a physical subsystem governed by silicon latency, transducer bandwidth, and mechanical dynamics. To operate as a **practical detector**\index{Practical detector!definition}, it must satisfy three tightly coupled engineering constraints:

1. **Statistical tail coverage**: High detection probability ($1 - \beta \ge 0.999$) across the heavy-tailed operational hazard distribution.
2. **Bounded false-alarm rate**: A false-positive rate low enough ($\alpha \le 10^{-4}$) to prevent alarm fatigue or unnecessary emergency stops that destroy warehouse throughput.
3. **Physical detection deadline**: Detection latency strictly shorter than the physical system's available reaction window:
   $$t_{\text{detect}} \le t_{\text{harm}} - (t_{\text{enforce}} + t_{\text{actuation}} + t_{\text{brake}}).$$

At the `{python} OilFilm.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, the finished stopping budget of @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget leaves the mobile manipulator `{python} OilFilm.spare_aisle_str` of its clear distance unspent, which the machine covers in `{python} OilFilm.t_latest_str` (@sec-intervention-authority-transitions). A detector for an approaching worker at the rack end that adds more than `{python} OilFilm.t_latest_str` to the observation-and-inference path is not a detector for that hazard.

The floor-film detector faces an even stricter form of the same test. Its forward detection distance, less the travel incurred during its own sensing and inference latency, must cover the dry-floor stop to the film's leading edge. A classification report that arrives once the drive wheels have already crossed onto the film leaves a stopping distance of `{python} OilFilm.stop_oil_str` against the `{python} OilFilm.d_clear_str` clear distance. A detector that reports after the physical point of no return is merely an expensive post-mortem event logger. Producing an accurate neural classification label after crossing an irreversible kinetic threshold generates diagnostic telemetry for an incident report, but it cannot serve as a runtime safeguard.

### Observational indistinguishability and practical detector latency {#sec-frontier-observational-indistinguishability-sub}

The fundamental physical limit of runtime detection arises from observational indistinguishability. Consider two physical states of the world, $S_A$ and $S_B$. In state $S_A$, a commanded actuator trajectory $u(t)$ is completely safe. In state $S_B$, the identical trajectory $u(t)$ causes catastrophic structural fracture or human injury, requiring the permission path to intervene and command an immediate stop. The dynamics of the body impose a hard deadline:
$$t_{\text{deadline}} = t_{\text{harm}} - (t_{\text{enforce}} + t_{\text{actuation}} + t_{\text{brake}}),$$
determined by actuator response time, motor torque limits, and kinetic momentum, after which physical contact or mechanical yield cannot be prevented. If the telemetry history $y(t)$ provided by onboard instrumentation is identical for $S_A$ and $S_B$ across the entire interval $t \le t_{\text{deadline}}$, no algorithm operating on those observations can reliably distinguish the benign state from the hazardous one. Identical telemetry traces rule out a state-specific response before that deadline. A conservative action chosen for both states or a passive mechanical limit may still protect them, if its own clearance and force assumptions are valid.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_observational_indistinguishability_chain.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Causal chain showing state split producing identical telemetry until deadline passes and irreversible damage occurs."}

*Identical pre-contact telemetry prevents software intervention before irreversible physical damage occurs.*
:::

To formalize this physical boundary where software anomaly detectors fail because incoming telemetry provides zero distinguishing energy before the action deadline, we state the principle of **observational indistinguishability** (\ref{dfn-frontier-observational-indistinguishability}):

::: {#dfn-frontier-observational-indistinguishability .callout-definition title="Observational indistinguishability"}
***Observational indistinguishability***\index{Observational indistinguishability!definition}\index{Detectorless failure!indistinguishability} is the physical condition where two distinct world states, one nominal ($S_A$) and one hazardous ($S_B$), generate identical pre-harm sensor telemetry ($y_A(t) \equiv y_B(t)$) up to the system's physical action deadline ($t_{\text{deadline}} = t_{\text{harm}} - t_{\text{act}}$).

1.  **Significance**: Without distinguishing physical energy prior to the action deadline, timely algorithmic differentiation is physically and mathematically impossible. Scaling neural model parameters, increasing dataset size, or accelerating inference compute cannot separate states that emit zero distinguishing physical energy before the time-to-harm.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike epistemic uncertainty or high classifier entropy (which signals that the model knows it lacks evidence), observational indistinguishability often pairs with high output confidence and near-zero entropy because the neural network maps corrupted observations into nominal latent manifolds.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Relying on software anomaly detectors or VAE reconstruction loss to catch detectorless degradation. When sensor physics blinds the transducer, as piezoresistive crystal creep does, or the hazardous state lies outside the sensed path, as a weakened latch does for the joint channel, the anomaly detector consumes telemetry that carries no trace of the fault and fails silently.
:::

The mathematical foundation of this limit is governed by the **Data Processing Inequality**\index{Data Processing Inequality!sensory channels}. Let $S \in \{S_A, S_B\}$ represent the true physical state of the world, $Y = g(S)$ represent the raw digitized sensor telemetry transmitted across the causal boundary into silicon, and $Z = f_\theta(Y)$ represent internal latent representations, feature maps, or anomaly scores computed by a deep neural network. The mutual information $\mathcal{I}(S; Z)$ between the physical state and the neural representation satisfies:
$$\mathcal{I}(S; Z) \le \mathcal{I}(S; Y).$$
If the physical transducer channel $\mathcal{Y}$ carries zero mutual information with the hazard state ($\mathcal{I}(S; Y) = 0$)—because optical photons reflect identically from dry concrete and thin hydraulic fluid, or because joint torque sensors read the identical contact force against a weakened latch as against a sound one—no downstream neural transformation, multi-modal foundation model, or variational autoencoder (VAE) reconstruction loss can synthesize that missing information:
$$\mathcal{I}(S; Y) = 0 \implies \mathcal{I}(S; Z) = 0.$$
The Brain cannot detect its own transducerless blindness.

In a learned perception-action policy, this same limit appears as **shortcut learning**\index{Shortcut learning!causal confusion}. A Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation model [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2] or a diffusion policy [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] minimizes empirical imitation loss on demonstration datasets using whatever correlations the training data contain. Where surface friction, material yield strength, or payload inertia goes unobserved by sensors, the network latches onto non-causal visual features—such as ambient lighting reflections, floor coloration, or background shadows—as spurious proxies. Under distribution shift in the field, these proxies fail abruptly. Yet the neural encoder continues mapping the unfamiliar observation into a familiar region of its latent manifold, causing the policy to command aggressive motions with high softmax confidence and near-zero ensemble variance. An uncertainty estimate computed from that same latent representation—whether a Mahalanobis distance, Monte Carlo dropout variance, or autoencoder reconstruction residual—inherits the exact same blindness. The proposal engine cannot detect its own shortcut failure, which is why physical containment must reside in the deterministic Nervous System below the proposal boundary.

In high-dexterity manipulation, observational indistinguishability manifests dynamically at the contact interface. When grasping a smooth or deformable object, contact mechanics is governed by Cattaneo-Mindlin partial slip theory: gross slip does not occur simultaneously across the entire contact patch, but initiates as a microscopic annular shear ring that propagates inward from the contact perimeter as tangential force approaches the Coulomb limit ($F_T \to \mu F_N$). External RGB cameras and low-bandwidth joint torque sensors observe zero macroscopic displacement ($y_A(t) \equiv y_B(t)$) during this partial slip phase. By the time macroscopic slip occurs, the object is already undergoing unconstrained gravitational acceleration ($g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$). Because camera exposure, deserialization, and neural inference impose an unavoidable latency of at least $50\text{ to }100\text{ ms}$, the physical action deadline $t_{\text{deadline}}$ is violated before any vision-based detector can trigger. Detecting slip before loss of control requires high-density tactile taxels measuring high-frequency micro-vibrations ($> 500\text{ Hz}$) and elastomeric shear strain directly at the skin interface.

### Passive compliance, structural containment, and proof-testing {#sec-frontier-passive-compliance-containment}

When physical states are observationally indistinguishable, software intervention is impossible. Safety must instead be guaranteed through mechanical compliance, physical proof-testing, or structural isolation.

Sensing hardware shows the same limit over longer durations. A robot's wrist force-torque transducer drifts as mechanical stress relaxation and temperature cycles affect its piezoresistive strain gauges, and a transducer whose zero has drifted low reports the same trend as an interaction that genuinely exerts lower contact force. A single channel reports one scalar wrench component, and no algorithm on that signal can tell a changed physical interaction from a degraded calibration baseline. Without an independent physical tare routine or a zero-point proof test, the drift is undetectable at runtime.[^fn-hw-piezoresistive-drift]

[^fn-hw-piezoresistive-drift]: **Piezoresistive Transducer Drift**\index{Piezoresistive transducer!drift}: Mechanical stress relaxation, adhesive creep, and temperature cycles alter the piezoresistive bridge balance of silicon strain gauges in robotic wrist sensors over extended campaigns. Monolithic software filters cannot separate slow baseline voltage drift from true contact force increments, creating an unobservable state transition. Preventing excessive contact forces therefore requires independent physical tare routines, unloaded zero-point proof-tests, or dual-dissimilar sensing architectures.

The weakened latch at the door is the arm's case of the same limit, and a faster one. Until the latch yields, the joint torque sensors read the same torques against a weakened latch as against a sound one, because both carry the same contact force, and the channel holds no trace of the strength that remains. The yield is irreversible, and no command issued after it restores the latch, so a faster classifier on the joint torque channel protects nothing. The defensible responses supply what that channel lacks. A proof test establishes the latch's strength at a declared interval, and it covers the interval only if corrosion and wear cannot carry the yield force below the contact ceiling between two tests, a rate that the maintenance record, not the torque channel, must support.

A passive compliant buffer in the wrist mechanically clamps contact force below the structural yield limit across a bounded deflection stroke, converting what would be an instantaneous rigid impact spike into a gradual force rise that buys critical time for safety watchdogs to cut motor current. When an unyielding metal tool or robotic link strikes a rigid obstacle at velocity $v$, rigid-body contact dynamics produce impact durations on the order of $\Delta t \approx 1\text{ to }2\text{ ms}$—vastly faster than the execution period of even a $1\text{ kHz}$ software control loop. In geared electric actuators, the effective impact inertia is dominated by the motor rotor reflected through the square of the transmission gear ratio ($J_{\text{reflected}} = N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}$). For high-reduction planetary, cycloidal, or harmonic gearboxes ($N \ge 100$), reflected inertia is ten thousand times rotor inertia ($100^2 = 10{,}000$). At the instant of collision, acoustic stress waves propagate through mechanical linkages at the speed of sound in aluminum ($c \approx 5{,}000\text{ m/s}$), producing destructive peak impact forces within microseconds ($< 500\,\mu\text{s}$) before any industrial communication bus (CAN-FD at $1\text{ ms}$ or EtherCAT at $250\,\mu\text{s}$) can transmit a single packet to the CPU. Introducing a Series Elastic Actuator (SEA) or passive mechanical spring buffer transforms these impact dynamics: the mechanical spring mechanically decouples the high reflected rotor inertia from the impact interface, causing force to build continuously at $\dot{F} = k_{\text{spring}} v$ and buying a physical reaction window of:
$$\Delta t_{\text{reaction}} = \frac{\Delta x_{\text{stall}}}{v}.$$
For an end-effector approaching at $v = 0.20\text{ m/s}$ with an available compliance stroke of $\Delta x_{\text{stall}} = 20.0\text{ mm}$, the mechanical spring buys $\Delta t_{\text{reaction}} = 100\text{ ms}$ of reaction margin—permitting dozens of control cycles for the deterministic Nervous System to detect contact and de-energize motor windings before force reaches destructive levels. @Eq-frontier-passive-compliance bounds this buffer stiffness, ensuring that full stroke deflection does not breach the latch's structural floor:[^fn-math-contact-lipschitz]
$$k_{\text{spring}} \le \frac{F_{\text{allow}}-F_{\text{preload}}}{\Delta x_{\text{stall}}}$$ {#eq-frontier-passive-compliance}
where $F_{\text{allow}}$ is the structural yield threshold of the workpiece, $F_{\text{preload}}$ is the preload resisting nominal manipulation forces, and $\Delta x_{\text{stall}}$ is the compliance stroke available before cutting drive power. If the buffer is sized too stiff or bottoms out against a mechanical hard stop, contact forces surge abruptly into rigid impact, shearing the mechanism without ever registering a distinguishable software signature.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Failures undetectable by sensory telemetry challenge the observation contracts formulated in @sec-perception-observation-contract.
:::

[^fn-math-contact-lipschitz]: **Contact Boundary**\index{Contact mechanics!non-smooth impact}: Rigid impact and friction transitions can invalidate a smooth free-motion model. Peak contact force and component damage require measured stiffness, damping, geometry, and actuator response; neither a controller nor a passive part alone supplies a universal bound.

The Cruise San Francisco collision failed in the opposite way from the Tempe collision of @sec-boundary-when-fails, where the sensors had detected the pedestrian but a designed suppression withheld the braking that state warranted. In San Francisco, an automated fallback maneuver acted, but on a physical state that no sensor reported.[^fn-case-cruise-inquiry] A faster trigger or broader authority would not have prevented the injury, because no measurement separated the state the fallback was qualified for from the actual one. A timelier response rule and a restored redundant brake path address a failure like Tempe's. Only qualification and sensing extended to every physical state the fallback may meet can repair the other kind, the detectorless failure this section describes and the one the oil film poses on the aisle.

[^fn-case-cruise-inquiry]: **Cruise Investigation Findings**\index{Incident postmortem!Cruise San Francisco}: The California DMV Order of Suspension and subsequent technical root-cause audits [@exponent2024cruise; @quinnemanuel2024cruise] established that the automated pullover maneuver treated perimeter sensor clearance as proof of an unobstructed path. This operational failure formalizes the requirement that fallback maneuvers must never inject mechanical power when the workspace beneath the chassis remains unobservable.

\Needspace{0.57\textheight}

::: {#ws-frontier-cruise-sf-blind-spot-post-collision .callout-war-story title="Cruise post-collision fallback failure (2023)"}
**Context**: On October 2, 2023, in San Francisco, a human-driven vehicle struck a pedestrian, launching them into an adjacent lane directly in front of an autonomous Cruise robotaxi [@exponent2024cruise; @quinnemanuel2024cruise].

**Mechanism**: The robotaxi's perception system detected the incoming obstacle and commanded emergency braking, coming to a halt directly over the pedestrian. The vehicle's collision detection subsystem recognized that a crash had occurred. However, perimeter cameras and lidar arrays could not observe the volume directly beneath the vehicle floorboard ($y_A(t) \equiv y_B(t)$ between clear asphalt and a person pinned under the carriage). The vehicle's post-collision maneuver software, designed to clear active traffic lanes after minor impacts, classified the lane ahead as unobstructed and commanded a pull-over to the curb. The vehicle accelerated, dragging the trapped pedestrian $20\text{ feet}$ ($6\text{ meters}$) along the road before stopping.

**Impact**: The pedestrian suffered severe traumatic injuries. The California Department of Motor Vehicles immediately suspended Cruise's autonomous testing and deployment permits, citing safety risk and misrepresentation of post-collision sensor capabilities, prompting Cruise to halt all commercial fleet operations.

**Response**: The independent technical root-cause analysis [@exponent2024cruise] established that the post-collision software lacked an accurate model of undercarriage occlusion and failed to verify that the under-vehicle region was clear before initiating motion. Cruise issued a software recall for its collision-response system to prohibit post-collision pullover maneuvers when sensor coverage is incomplete.

**Systems lesson**: The physical state beneath the chassis was unobservable to the sensor suite ($y_A(t) \equiv y_B(t)$). The fallback procedure was verified only under the unstated premise that accident victims remain within perimeter sensor coverage. When an unexpected physical trajectory violated that premise, an automated safety routine acted on an unobserved reality, escalating a survivable incident into a catastrophic injury. Automated fallbacks must never inject mechanical power when critical safety states lie in an unobservable subspace. **The Undercarriage Blind Spot Invariant** establishes that an autonomous machine must never command motion when critical safety state lies in an unobservable sensory subspace.
:::

When a failure mode lacks a practical detector, the remaining responses are to limit actuator authority under a validated force or clearance model, restrict the operating domain, add independent sensing, or schedule proof tests. A force limit rests on that validated model, because ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066 apply to their industrial robot scopes and supply no universal force limit for this machine. Active sensing is itself actuation. A small dither of the wheels, an active probe for the film, measures traction only where the wheels already are, so it cannot close the friction entry. Because the probe must not slip beyond the reserved clearance, the independent permission path must admit each probe command within a separately validated energy, contact, clearance, and timing envelope and choose a state-matched fallback when the needed bound is unavailable. If none of these measures can support the claim, operation must be withheld.

The safety case must document these gaps. @Fig-17-epistemic-limits marks where the argument runs out. The residual-claims register records the detector's blind region, defining the set of physical states that produce indistinguishable observations, along with the maximum exposure duration permitted between physical proof tests. Treating an undetectable failure as a solved runtime problem undermines the validity of the safety case. Preserving the exact boundary where sensing stops forces the engineering organization to rely on physical constraints rather than software optimism.

::: {#fig-17-epistemic-limits fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Two limits on the claim**: Panel (a) shows states with identical pre-deadline telemetry. A speed clamp is useful only with a supported braking and clearance envelope. Panel (b) shows the zero-event exposure required for a rare-rate claim under the chosen Poisson model; a barrier argument also needs observable state, a feasible control action, and valid timing assumptions." fig-alt="Panel (a) shows safe and hazardous states producing the same telemetry until after the action deadline, with a conditional speed clamp. Panel (b) shows zero-event exposure growing inversely with the target rate and a conditional barrier argument."}
![](images/svg/fig17_epistemic_limits.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Panel (a) shows safe and hazardous states producing the same telemetry until after the action deadline, with a conditional speed clamp. Panel (b) shows zero-event exposure growing inversely with the target rate and a conditional barrier argument."}
:::

The two panels of @fig-17-epistemic-limits synthesize the twin boundaries that govern physical AI dependability:

1. **Panel (a) Observational Boundary**: The horizontal time axis traces the evolution of two physically distinct paths: a safe nominal state $S_{\text{safe}}$ (blue curve) and an impending hazardous state $S_{\text{hazard}}$ (red curve)—such as a mobile robot traversing dry concrete vs. approaching an invisible hydraulic fluid film. Throughout the critical pre-deadline window enclosed by the dashed yellow box, both states produce strictly identical telemetry:
   $$y_A(t) \equiv y_B(t) \quad \forall t \le t_{\text{deadline}}.$$
   Because standard camera and lidar channels cannot detect the low-friction film under ambient warehouse lighting, the permission path remains entirely unaware of the degradation. At $t_{\text{deadline}}$, the physical point of no return is crossed: given the robot's loaded momentum, braking must commence immediately to avoid overrunning the aisle end. However, physical detection only occurs at $t_{\text{detect}} > t_{\text{deadline}}$ when the drive wheels begin slipping under braking. As marked by the **State ID late** callout, by the time the state discrepancy is recognized, stopping distance already exceeds available clearance. Under observational indistinguishability, software perception cannot protect the machine; safety must instead be guaranteed through **Structural Containment**—clamping operating velocity to a restricted envelope $v \le v_{\text{clamp}}$ sized such that unbraked slide remains within clear margins if the friction floor $\mu$ holds.

2. **Panel (b) Exposure Wall**: The log-log hyperbola traces the required continuous zero-failure operational hours $n$ across target failure rates $p$, governed by the Poisson Rule of Three ($n \ge 3.0 / p$ at 95 percent confidence). As the target failure rate drops from routine industrial anomalies ($p = 10^{-3}\ \text{h}^{-1}$, requiring $3{,}000$ zero-failure hours) to civil aviation and functional safety standards ($p = 10^{-9}\ \text{h}^{-1}$, 1 FIT), required test exposure escalates to an astronomical $3 \times 10^9$ hours (over $340{,}000$ continuous vehicle-years). To escape this empirical exposure wall, engineers rely on **Barrier Invariants**—mathematically certifying forward invariance ($h(x) \ge 0$) via control barrier functions (@sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission). However, as highlighted in the green panel footer, a barrier invariant guarantees safety *only if two physical premises hold*: the full state $x(t)$ must be observable from sensors $y(t)$, and the certified control action $u^*(t)$ must be physically feasible within motor torque and thermal saturation bounds. If state observability fails (as in Panel a) or torque saturates, the mathematical barrier collapses.

Each detectorless mode still leaves a defensible response, and @tbl-17-detectorless-modes sets four of them side by side.[^fn-hw-motor-thermal]

[^fn-hw-motor-thermal]: **Motor Thermal State**\index{Actuator!stator thermal dynamics}: Winding resistance and magnet flux can change with temperature. Whether that changes braking authority depends on the drive, current limits, load, and measured thermal model; a separate holding path may be required for gravity-loaded axes.

| Failure and missing state                                                                            | Why the existing channel can miss it                                                              | Deadline or evidence deficit                                                                                              | Defensible response                                                                                                                      |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Pressure-sensor drift**: zero offset changes with aging or deposition.                             | One channel cannot separate true pressure change from its own offset drift.                       | Drift may persist until the process reaches its pressure limit; a detector cannot be credited without a second reference. | Independent calibrated pressure channel, proof test, and rated relief path.                                                              |
| **Latch-strength loss**: corrosion or wear lowers the latch's yield force below the contact ceiling. | Joint torque sensors read the same contact force against a weakened latch as against a sound one. | Latch strength is unmeasured between proof tests, and the yield is irreversible, so no later command restores the latch.  | A passive compliant element sized by @eq-frontier-passive-compliance to a declared floor on latch strength, or proof tests of the latch. |
| **Rotor flux loss**: delivered torque differs from current-based estimate.                           | Stator current alone does not measure the torque constant after magnet damage.                    | A gravity-loaded axis may have little time to arrest once available torque is lost.                                       | Measure torque or rotor state, derate within tested limits, and validate a holding or controlled-stop path.                              |
| **Learned perception shift**: an optical artifact is mistaken for a known scene.                     | Model confidence may remain high even while the physical scene differs.                           | Confidence or reconstruction loss alone does not bound clearance or stopping response.                                    | Independent range/clearance checks and an admitted motion envelope, with residual blind regions recorded.                                |

: **Detectorless physical failure taxonomy**: Four failure modes, in transduction, contact, the drive, and learned perception, whose safe and hazardous states look identical to the existing channel before the time-to-harm. For each, the table gives why the channel misses it, the deadline or evidence it cannot meet, and the response that still supports a claim. {#tbl-17-detectorless-modes tbl-colwidths="[23,26,24,27]"}

Every row fails the practical-detector test because the existing channel gives identical observations for the safe and hazardous states until the deadline has passed. Every defensible response supplies what that channel lacks: a second reference, a passive load limit, a direct torque measurement, or an independent range check. What that missing element is, and whether it can be built, decides the kind of gap each register entry records.

## Sensitivity to Foundational Modeling Assumptions {#sec-frontier-assumptions-change}

The three entries in the mobile manipulator's residual-claims register\index{Residual-claims register} lack the same element: a qualified detector for a state no sensor in service reports. Sorting every recorded gap by what is missing turns the register from an ad hoc list of caveats into an engineering agenda. To alter an operational release verdict, research advances must supply the missing evidence that directly discharges an open register entry.

### The four epistemological gap classes in embodied AI {#sec-frontier-four-gap-classes}

A recorded safety gap falls into one of four distinct classes, defined by the missing element. It stems from an **unmeasured observable**\index{Unmeasured observable} when the true physical state (such as a hidden internal defect) cannot be distinguished from sensor data before the deadline for action; from an **evaluation deficit**\index{Evaluation deficit} when the tail probability of failure cannot be bounded because these rare events require intractable physical exposure; from a **theoretical deficit**\index{Theoretical deficit} when the learned policy lacks a bounded relationship between training conditions and execution stability; or from a **scope mismatch**\index{Scope mismatch} when the target claim exceeds what the system architecture can physically support. All three of the machine's entries belong to the first class. More grounding-model trials at the pick station or more stopping runs on dry floors would treat them as evaluation deficits, which they are not. Naming the missing capability defines the exact physical or mathematical requirement that would discharge the entry.

Closing a gap from an unmeasured observable requires a new physical measurement that separates previously indistinguishable states within the permission path's deadline. For the film, a software filter or a learned estimator running on the navigation camera and the lidar cannot be that measurement, because it consumes the same observations that already fail to separate film from dry floor. The floor-film detector must respond to the film through an independent physical channel, and it closes the entry only if it meets the timing requirement of @sec-frontier-failures-without-detectors, holds a bounded false-alarm rate, and fails independently of the cameras.

Closing an evaluation deficit requires replacing raw sample counts with estimators whose bias and variance can be bounded analytically. Logging more unperturbed operation, or running simulated episodes whose fidelity in the tail is unverified, cannot bound a tail rate. An importance-sampling\index{Importance Sampling} or adaptive stress-testing\index{Adaptive Stress-Testing} scheme can, if it demonstrates conservative estimates on benchmark distributions whose answer is known and reports effective independent exposure rather than raw trial counts. Ten thousand simulated trajectories that explore one basin of a collision surface say little about the others, so effective sample size must be estimated from the weights and their dependence.

Closing a theoretical deficit requires a bounded analytical claim paired with a runtime mechanism that checks its premises. For a policy trained by imitation or reinforcement learning, the deficit is the absence of any guarantee of bounded outputs under distribution shift, and neither asymptotic convergence nor a bound resting on an uncheckable Lipschitz constant closes it. The theory must state the invariance it guarantees and the support over which it holds, and the machine must carry a monitor that flags when its state leaves that support, with bounded estimator error and decision delay and a validated state-matched stop.

In non-rigid deformable object manipulation—such as manipulating surgical tissue, routing high-voltage vehicle wiring harnesses, or seating elastomeric sealing gaskets—theoretical deficits and unmeasured observables merge. Classical mechanics models these interactions through finite element methods (FEM) or Cosserat rod formulations, but real-world elastomers exhibit non-linear viscoelastic hysteresis, internal frictional damping, and plastic strain hardening. An unprivileged policy trained via reinforcement learning or imitation learning operates under an unverified assumption of elastic restitution. When the material experiences micro-tearing or permanent plastic yield, the physical plant switches into an altered dynamical regime without exhibiting any preceding anomaly in visual telemetry. A candidate advance that claims to guarantee deformable manipulation safety via an idealized linear-elastic simulation merely shifts epistemic debt from neural policy weights to ungrounded physics engine parameters.

To prevent research optimism from corrupting the safety case, each candidate advance must undergo evaluation against a predeclared closure test. The test defines the missing argument link, the numerical threshold required for sufficiency, and the independent evidence necessary to verify it. An advance fails the test if it merely relocates an assumption to a less visible layer of the system. Systems engineers must guard against **Assumption Shifting (the conservation of epistemic debt)**\index{Epistemic debt!conservation}: replacing an opaque neural network controller with a "provably safe" control-barrier function whose certificate assumes perfectly known linear dynamics $\dot{x} = A x + B u$ does not eliminate epistemic uncertainty. It merely relocates the unmodeled dynamics from the opaque network weights to the unverified barrier derivative. If the physical plant experiences unobserved tire slip, actuator deadbands, or payload shifts, the formal certificate is just as ungrounded as the neural policy it was intended to safeguard. Epistemic debt cannot be eliminated by mathematical formalization; it can only be discharged by empirical physical evidence. A candidate advance is stopped before it can alter the safety verdict whenever its validation relies on the exact unverified properties it was designed to establish.

Closing a scope mismatch acknowledges that certain gaps cannot be closed by any known sensor, sampling regime, or mathematical framework. When physical laws, computational limits, or economic constraints preclude the necessary measurement or proof, the safety case cannot remain suspended in anticipation of future discovery. Narrowing the actuator's physical authority, restricting the operational design domain (ODD)\index{Operational design domain}, or refusing to operate the machine is not an admission of research defeat. It is the engineering resolution. Classical fault-tolerant design\index{Fault tolerance!structural bounds} reached the same conclusion, that dependable operation comes from self-monitoring thresholds\index{Self-Monitoring} and structural isolation\index{Structural Isolation} that contain faults rather than from eliminating every disturbance. An arm whose compliant wrist bounds contact force below a declared floor on latch strength does not need to detect a weakened latch to leave it intact. The residual-claims register records the boundary of verifiable knowledge, and the permission path and the machine's passive limits enforce the constraints that bound the consequence of what remains unknown.

Research directions in physical machine learning must therefore be judged solely by whether they convert an open residual claim into verified evidence capable of altering the operational verdict. General improvements on benchmark leaderboards, such as a 3 percent reduction in average tracking error or higher reward on a standard task suite, provide no evidence toward closing an unsupported safety link. A research project becomes relevant to physical deployment only when its deliverable targets a specific entry in the claims register, whether by providing the missing transducer, bounding the tail estimator, or furnishing the runtime-checked stability proof. If an advance improves mean performance but leaves the detector blind spot or the tail uncertainty unchanged, the authority limits of the machine remain exactly where they were.

### Extreme value theory and heavy-tailed risk estimation {#sec-frontier-evt-heavy-tails}

Evaluating safety tails in physical robotics requires rejecting naive Gaussian assumptions when attempting to close evaluation deficits. In classical statistics, the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) assumes that independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables sum to thin, exponentially decaying Gaussian tails: $P(X \ge x) \sim e^{-x^2 / (2\sigma^2)}$. Under a Gaussian distribution, an extreme $6\sigma$ deviation is an astronomical impossibility ($\approx 10^{-9}$ probability). In physical robotics, however, the CLT fails systematically due to three physical mechanisms:

1. **Nonlinear dynamic compounding**: Small tracking errors alter contact geometry or tire slip angles, nonlinearly amplifying dynamic yaw moments until the plant suddenly spins out.
2. **Coupled common-cause stressors**: Environmental shifts (such as a sudden downpour, blinding sunset glare, or floor grease) degrade camera contrast, lidar reflectivity, and wheel traction simultaneously.
3. **Discontinuous physical bifurcations**: Friction transitions from static adhesion to dynamic sliding, electrical buses brown out, or mechanical linkages yield, abruptly switching the system into an entirely different dynamical regime.

Because of these phenomena, physical robotics failures exhibit **heavy tails**\index{Heavy-tailed distributions!robotics failure modes}, where catastrophic outliers occur orders of magnitude more frequently than Gaussian models predict. To bound these rare events without waiting centuries for collisions, engineers apply **Extreme Value Theory (EVT)**\index{Extreme Value Theory!Generalized Pareto Distribution}. By the Pickands-Balkema-de Haan Theorem,[^fn-math-evt-convergence] tail excesses $Y = X - u$ over a sufficiently high threshold $u$ converge asymptotically to the Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD) formulated in @eq-frontier-generalized-pareto:
$$G_{\xi, \sigma}(y) = 1 - \left( 1 + \frac{\xi y}{\sigma} \right)^{-1/\xi}$$ {#eq-frontier-generalized-pareto}

[^fn-math-evt-convergence]: **Pickands-Balkema-de Haan Theorem**\index{Extreme Value Theory!asymptotic convergence}: The convergence of tail excesses $Y = X - u$ to the Generalized Pareto Distribution requires the underlying distribution to lie in the domain of attraction of an extreme value law as threshold $u \to x_F$. In physical robotics, threshold selection balances estimator variance against bias from non-tail dynamics (@sec-appendix-ml-evt).

where $\xi$ is the shape parameter (tail index), $\sigma$ is scale, and $y$ represents excess margin deficit beyond operational safety thresholds (such as peak deceleration shortfalls, tracking boundary overshoots, or transient contact overforces). When $\xi > 0$, the tail exhibits power-law decay ($y^{-1/\xi}$) rather than exponential decay. By fitting a GPD to sub-critical near-miss telemetry logged during canary fleet operations, engineers can mathematically extrapolate the probability of rare tail-event safety breaches without waiting for catastrophic failures to manifest in the field (@sec-appendix-ml-evt). When tail indices satisfy $\xi > 0$, the empirical exposure required to verify safety escalates dramatically, reinforcing why closure tests must be sized against heavy-tailed extreme-value distributions rather than ungrounded Gaussian assumptions.

### Continual on-device learning and multi-robot non-stationarity {#sec-frontier-continual-learning-multi-robot}

Two emerging systems challenges define the modern epistemic frontier of physical AI: adapting to non-stationary platform dynamics through lifelong on-device learning, and coordinating coupled fleets of autonomous machines.

In physical robotics, environments and mechanical bodies are non-stationary: tires wear down, linkages loosen, motor windings oxidize, and workspace layouts change. While modern deep learning relies on streaming gradient updates, executing lifelong continual learning directly on embedded robotic hardware encounters severe physical barriers:

1. **Activation memory and thermal dissipation limits**: Forward policy inference requires storing only the current layer activations in memory. Backpropagation, however, requires caching intermediate activations across the entire computational graph, increasing peak working memory by $3\times\text{ to }5\times$ and energy consumption per sample by $3\times$. In an IP65 sealed chassis with a strict $15\text{ to }60\,\text{W}$ thermal envelope, continuous on-device backpropagation triggers immediate silicon thermal throttling ($T_j \ge 105^\circ\text{C}$), degrading inference throughput and violating real-time control deadlines. On an autonomous mobile robot or humanoid, onboard compute shares a finite electrochemical battery capacity ($E_{\text{batt}} \le 500\text{ Wh}$) with propulsion and manipulation actuators. Running on-device gradient updates on an embedded GPU draws an additional $50\text{ to }100\text{ W}$, depleting mission endurance twice as fast. In high-dexterity manipulation or dynamic bipedal balancing, an unexpected thermal throttling event stretching inference latency from $20\text{ ms}$ to $100\text{ ms}$ immediately breaches the unbraked reaction corridor, converting an online learning update into catastrophic mechanical collision.
2. **Catastrophic forgetting and stability-plasticity collapse**: Gradient updates fine-tuned on recent local experiences (such as navigating a novel aisle geometry) catastrophically overwrite edge-case safety reflexes learned during extensive pretraining.
3. **Exposure clock and certificate invalidation**: Any on-device weight modification $\theta \to \theta + \Delta \theta$ alters the proposal distribution. Under the Poisson exposure model and formal neural barrier certificate frameworks ($\alpha,\beta$-CROWN), **an unverified weight update instantly resets the empirical exposure clock to zero and mathematically invalidates the barrier certificate**. Continual adaptation on hardware therefore demands isolated parameter adapters (e.g., low-rank LoRA heads), immutable safety-envelope baselines, and episodic shadow-mode canary verification.

Coupled multi-robot systems introduce a parallel epistemic boundary. In warehouse fleets and collaborative manufacturing, autonomous agents share physical workspace:

- **Decentralized epistemic horizons**: When Robot A executes an admitted motion, it changes the physical environment for Robot B. If Robot A encounters an unobserved oil film and enters an extended skid, it becomes an unmodeled dynamic obstacle for Robot B.
- **Asymmetric wireless latency and packet drops**: Multi-robot coordination cannot rely on a shared-memory bus. Wireless jitter and packet drops ($20\text{ to }200\text{ ms}$) mean every agent plans on stale, out-of-sync state observations of other agents.
- **Liveness vs. safety deadlocks**: Conservative local Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) that guarantee pairwise collision avoidance frequently induce emergent fleet deadlocks (e.g., four mobile manipulators freezing at an intersection, each waiting for another to yield). Verifying liveness and safety simultaneously across coupled multi-agent systems remains one of the grand open challenges of physical ML systems.

The register, the practical-detector test, and the four gap classes have so far been applied to machines whose records already existed. The method must also hold for a machine with no records yet, where the engineer has to decide which premises to measure, which to restrict, and which to leave open.

## Generalizing to Unfamiliar Systems {#sec-frontier-generalizing-unfamiliar-systems}

Applied in sequence to any physical machine not previously examined, the four bedrock laws of @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws serve as fundamental systems invariants. They isolate physical hazards, compute kinetic reaction corridors, and establish architectural containment boundaries before hardware is energized. When confronting an unfamiliar physical machine—whether an automated logistics workcell, an autonomous mining hauler, or a collaborative humanoid robot—the traditional machine learning instinct is to ask: *What foundation model should we fine-tune? What loss function should we optimize? How many teleoperated demonstrations must we collect?* The systems discipline inverts this entire hierarchy. Before asking what the statistical model can propose, the systems engineer must audit what the physical machine can irreversibly destroy. The Four Bedrock Laws are not speculative guidelines; they are mathematically enforceable physical invariants. Applying them in disciplined sequence establishes the hard physical perimeter within which unprivileged learned policies can operate safely.

### The four-law audit protocol for novel physical systems {#sec-frontier-four-law-audit-protocol}

Before energizing an unfamiliar machine or loading learned weights into an industrial workcell, systems engineers execute a disciplined four-law diagnostic audit:

1. **Step 1: Irreversibility Audit (Law 1)**: Catalog all physical state changes that cannot be reversed by motor inversion (plastic deformation, component fracture, workcell intrusion, thermal insulation breakdown). Map the full sensor-to-actuator pipeline latency ($\tau_{\text{delay}} = t_{\text{exp}} + t_{\text{inf}} + t_{\text{bus}} + t_{\text{act}}$) across the physical AI stack—from camera exposure and direct memory access (DMA) transfers to RTOS scheduling, CAN-FD/EtherCAT bus latency, and Field-Oriented Control (FOC) electrical time constants. In whole-body dynamic locomotion, evaluate centroidal momentum $h_{\text{com}} = [m v_{\text{com}}^T, L_{\text{com}}^T]^T$ and dynamic capture points: once the center of mass exits the capture recovery basin under motor torque saturation ($\tau \le \tau_{\max}$), gravity induces irreversible toppling. Establish whether total stopping distance or balance recovery fits within available spatial clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$).
2. **Step 2: Endogenous Data Audit (Law 2)**: Identify all closed-loop proposal generators whose actions alter downstream sensory observations ($s_{t+1} \sim P(s_{t+1} \mid s_t, a_t)$). Trace how compounding drift ($O(T^2 \epsilon)$), non-rigid object deformation, and physical contact shocks shift the sensory distribution. Verify whether operational restrictions or derated modes move the models outside their evaluation Operational Design Domain (ODD).
3. **Step 3: Proposal is not Permission Audit (Law 3)**: Implement an independent, deterministic Nervous System permission path executing at high frequency ($1\text{ kHz}$) on isolated silicon. Decouple unprivileged multi-modal foundation models from low-level execution: pass proposed trajectories through a real-time quadratic program (QP) enforcing Control Barrier Functions, joint torque limits, and friction cone constraints ($|F_T| \le \mu F_N$) before dispatching commands to 20-50 kHz FOC motor inverters. Equip this path with dedicated hardware Safe Torque Off (STO) relays and independent physical fallbacks that cannot be bypassed, pre-empted, or delayed by the proposal engine.
4. **Step 4: Evidence Bounds Authority Audit (Law 4)**: Construct the residual-claims register. For every link where sensory observation is indistinguishable ($y_A \equiv y_B$), where contact friction or material elasticity is unmeasured, where empirical exposure is bounded by the Poisson wall, or where formal verification hits dimensional ceilings, refuse normal release and enforce conditional operational restrictions (signed velocity clamps, force limiters, exclusionary geofences) until predeclared closure tests pass.

### Multi-archetype case study on automated packaging cells {#sec-frontier-packaging-cell-study}

To see the four-law audit protocol in operation, consider an automated parcel induction and sortation cell in a logistics hub. The machine shuttles containers along a linear track, presses an articulated insertion head onto container flaps to engage structural retention tabs, and drives high-rate linear servo drives during high-throughput transfer. This workcell couples all three machine classes of @sec-boundary-three-classes within a single enclosure: the carriage as moving mass, the insertion head as contact force, and the high-duty actuator drives as thermal dissipation.

The first law asks what the cell cannot undo, so the evaluation begins by cataloging the irreversible state changes\index{State change!irreversible} the cell can produce and the physical bounds\index{Physical bounds} that govern them. A loaded parcel container traversing a linear transfer rail carries momentum. When a carriage strikes an obstruction, kinetic energy is dissipated through plastic deformation of the container and structural deflection of the frame, a state transition that cannot be reversed by commanding the drive motor in reverse. The insertion mechanism introduces a second irreversible boundary. An actuator drives a mechanical tool head against package tabs to lock retaining clips. If the actuator exerts force beyond the compressive yield strength of the carton wall, the container buckles, crushing internal contents. The high-duty drive introduces a third irreversible boundary through Joule heating ($I^2 R$). Continuous high-acceleration cycles pump thermal energy into sealed motor windings; once stator insulation melts or winding enamel degrades under excessive thermal exposure, cooling the housing cannot restore winding dielectric integrity.

Because the carriage's momentum is already committed, the permission path must act before the carriage consumes its clearance. Consider, with illustrative values throughout, a linear carriage of mass $m_{\text{carriage}} = 12.0\text{ kg}$ transporting a loaded tray at a nominal velocity of $v_{\text{nom}} = 1.50\text{ m/s}$ toward an optical inspection station whose mechanical gate provides a physical clearance margin of $D_{\text{clear}} = 60.0\text{ mm}$ before contacting a rigid frame stop. An overhead vision system detects a closing inspection gate. The controller commands an electromagnetic track brake with a credible deceleration of $a_{\text{brake}} = 15.0\text{ m/s}^2$, a value that assumes the pad and rail friction stay as tested. Determining whether an onboard vision system can halt the carriage prior to an impact requires computing the pre-brake delay $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ across the full observation-to-braking path. This delay spans optical exposure and rolling-shutter integration ($t_{\text{exp}} = 16.0\text{ ms}$), DMA transfer and neural detection inference ($t_{\text{inf}} = 36.0\text{ ms}$), CAN-FD safety arbitration bus latency ($t_{\text{bus}} = 2.0\text{ ms}$), and brake solenoid flux buildup rise time ($t_{\text{sol}} = 10.0\text{ ms}$):
$$\tau_{\text{delay}} = t_{\text{exp}} + t_{\text{inf}} + t_{\text{bus}} + t_{\text{sol}} = 16.0 + 36.0 + 2.0 + 10.0 = 64.0\text{ ms} = 0.064\text{ s}.$$
Over this delay, the carriage travels blind for:
$$d_{\text{blind}} = v_{\text{nom}} \tau_{\text{delay}} = 1.50\text{ m/s} \times 0.064\text{ s} = 96.0\text{ mm}.$$
This blind travel alone exceeds the $D_{\text{clear}} = 60.0\text{ mm}$ physical clearance, so the physical deadline is missed before mechanical braking even begins. Once the solenoid engages, deceleration consumes an additional distance:
$$d_{\text{brake}} = \frac{v_{\text{nom}}^2}{2 a_{\text{brake}}} = \frac{(1.50\text{ m/s})^2}{2 \times 15.0\text{ m/s}^2} = 75.0\text{ mm}.$$
The composite stopping distance is the sum of both terms:
$$d_{\text{stop}} = d_{\text{blind}} + d_{\text{brake}} = 96.0\text{ mm} + 75.0\text{ mm} = 171.0\text{ mm}.$$
That stop exceeds the physical clearance by a severe stopping deficit of:
$$\Delta d = d_{\text{stop}} - D_{\text{clear}} = 171.0\text{ mm} - 60.0\text{ mm} = 111.0\text{ mm}.$$
The machine cannot stop before the modeled gate at this velocity by relying on that vision path.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Closed-loop rollouts, distribution shift, and endogenous data generation are developed in @sec-data and @sec-evaluation.
:::

The second law asks what the cell's learned proposers have shown they can do. Three of them propose actions here, one in each domain. A vision model infers container contents to propose carriage transit speeds, a multimodal network estimates packaging cardboard thickness to propose insertion forces and dwell durations, and an electro-thermal estimator proposes acceleration profiles to manage motor winding temperatures. Each proposer's actions choose part of what it observes next. A slower carriage changes the motion blur and timing of the frames the vision model sees, a longer dwell changes the deformation that the next thickness estimate reads, and an acceleration profile changes the temperature trajectory the thermal estimator receives. Their competence therefore extends only to the states a closed-loop evaluation covered, and the question for this cell is whether the target ODD of its evaluation record contains the states that operation will admit. A restriction imposed after training is itself a change of operating condition. If the demonstrations were collected at the nominal transit speed, the derated mode that the cell's release claim requires moves the vision model into conditions its evaluation never sampled, so the restriction that shortens the stop also opens a regime without evidence. Either the evaluation samples the restricted mode before release, or the release claim records that regime as an open premise.

The third law places those proposals beneath an authority split\index{Authority split} that the proposers cannot delay or corrupt. The permission path keeps the proposals from reaching actuators directly. Its independent kinematic check, at $1\text{ kHz}$, monitors optical encoders along the track, admitting carriage velocity only where rangefinder coverage, measured gate clearance, and a validated stop path support the envelope. For the insertion head, a mechanical force limiter caps transmitted force at a selected $220\text{ N}$, a cap that holds only while the limiter's calibration does. For the drive motors, an independent thermal sensor trips a hardware power relay when measured winding temperature reaches $105^\circ\text{C}$ or continuous stall current exceeds $400\text{ ms}$. In the Field-Oriented Control (FOC) inverter, rapid deceleration dumps kinetic energy back into the DC bus via regenerative braking ($P_{\text{regen}} = \tau \omega$); a dedicated brake chopper circuit shunts excess current into a power resistor to prevent bus overvoltage tripping ($V_{\text{dc}} \ge 60\text{ V}$) that would otherwise disable the inverter during an emergency stop. The learned policy retains authority to optimize throughput and placement quality within these bounds, but the permission path retains sole authority to permit physical execution.

The fourth law turns what the evidence supports into a release claim\index{Release claim} and names what it leaves open. The evidence record\index{Evidence record} can support a restricted kinetic claim after tests of rangefinder coverage, gate clearance, and braking. The firmware velocity clamp is sized from the same stopping distance. Requiring the stop to fit within the physical clearance with a safety margin of $d_{\text{margin}} \ge 15.0\text{ mm}$ imposes the constraint $d_{\text{stop}}(v) \le 45.0\text{ mm}$. Reducing operational velocity shortens both terms. Derating velocity threefold, from $v_{\text{nom}} = 1.50\text{ m/s}$ to a firmware clamp of $v_{\text{clamp}} \le 0.50\text{ m/s}$, compresses blind travel linearly:
$$d_{\text{blind}} = 0.50\text{ m/s} \times 0.064\text{ s} = 32.0\text{ mm},$$
while braking distance falls quadratically:
$$d_{\text{brake}} = \frac{(0.50\text{ m/s})^2}{2 \times 15.0\text{ m/s}^2} \approx 8.3\text{ mm}.$$
The composite stopping distance:
$$d_{\text{stop}} = d_{\text{blind}} + d_{\text{brake}} = 32.0\text{ mm} + 8.3\text{ mm} = 40.3\text{ mm} \le 45.0\text{ mm}$$
comfortably fits within the $45.0\text{ mm}$ threshold, preserving a $19.7\text{ mm}$ physical margin. Simultaneously, carriage kinetic energy drops quadratically by 88.9 percent:
$$E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2: 13.5\text{ J} \to 1.50\text{ J}.$$

Assembling the evidence record also uncovers claims that remain unsupported. To assess flap latching integrity, the engineering team evaluates a vision model that inspects optical surface reflections for container tab engagement. Under overhead illumination, localized plastic wrap reflections and tape glare create optical artifacts that mimic latch defects while masking genuine tab misalignments. Because no independent physical sensor exists in the cell to measure tab engagement force directly in real time under glare, this claim has no practical detector. Marking this link as detectorless and unsupported in the claims register\index{Claims register} is not an omission in the documentation, but an accurate statement of what the evidence can justify.

The derated stop therefore supports a *candidate restricted mode* for transport at $0.50\text{ m/s}$, provided the stated 64 ms end-to-end delay, $15\text{ m/s}^2$ credible deceleration, and $60\text{ mm}$ clearance are validated together. Insertion and thermal management remain conditional on tests of the force limiter, thermal cutoff, material limits, and independent fault path. Autonomous package sign-off is refused because optical glare can conceal tab misalignments from the available vision sensor and the cell has not established latch engagement independently. That link could be closed by an independent tactile probe, a calibrated tare-force verification, or mandatory downstream inspection. A throughput model cannot replace that physical evidence.

The evaluation of the cell did not begin with model architecture, training losses, or benchmark scores. It began at the physical body, where mass, force, and energy create irreversible state changes, and it ended with an evidence record that marks its open links and restricts authority to what the evidence supports. A neural network predicting a high probability of a safe stop will still crash if the brakes cannot engage before the clearance is consumed.

## Open Architectural Challenges Beyond the Four Bedrock Laws {#sec-frontier-architectural-synthesis}

The four bedrock laws formalize the irreversible physics, endogenous distribution shift, asymmetric proposal boundaries, and temporal ceilings governing physical AI systems. Yet bridging these foundational principles to generalist autonomous machines operating in open-world physical environments exposes critical architectural frontiers where machine learning systems, embedded hardware, and real-time execution intersect.

### The four grand open ML systems challenges {#sec-frontier-four-open-challenges}

Translating the four bedrock laws into scalable deployment defines four foundational research and systems challenges for machine learning engineers:

1. **Deterministic Low-Latency VLA Serving**: Modern Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models scale parameter counts from 7B to 70B parameters, exhibiting inference latencies of $100\text{ to }500\,\text{ms}$ on workstation GPUs. On mobile robot platforms, however, that delay translates into massive unbraked blind travel ($d_{\text{blind}} = v \cdot t_{\text{inf}}$) and violates real-time reaction deadlines. In high-dexterity manipulation, the challenge is intensified by multi-modal sensor fusion: a robot must concurrently process multi-view RGB streams (30 to 60 Hz), high-resolution optical tactile elastomeric arrays (such as GelSight or DIGIT sensors streaming contact deformation at 60 to 120 Hz), and 6-axis joint torque/IMU streams at 1 kHz. Edge execution operates at streaming batch size 1, severely throttled by the memory wall ($f \le B/M$, @sec-brain-memory-wall). Achieving closed-loop dexterity requires hardware-software co-design: specialized edge NPUs with on-chip SRAM caches, speculative action chunking (where high-level VLAs generate intent tokens at 5 Hz while fast diffusion or linear policies unroll action chunks at 50 Hz, smoothed by 1 kHz $C^2$ quintic spline filters on safety MCUs), and aggressive 4-bit/8-bit weight-activation quantization that preserves spatial precision within a strict $15\text{ to }60\,\text{W}$ IP65 chassis thermal envelope.
2. **Hardware-Accelerated Neural Barrier Verification**: While branch-and-bound verification frameworks ($\alpha,\beta$-CROWN) relax the exponential Grid Wall, verifying forward-invariant neural barrier certificates for high-dimensional robotic plants ($d > 30$) remains orders of magnitude too slow for online deployment. In whole-body dynamic locomotion, where contact switches and impulsive ground reaction forces demand instantaneous barrier re-synthesis within milliseconds, existing GPUs and NPUs are fundamentally mismatched: they are optimized for dense matrix multiplications, not the tree-search linear relaxation operations required by formal solvers. Bridging this gap requires co-designing specialized hardware accelerators for bound propagation (Interval Bound Propagation and Linear Relaxation-based Perturbation Analysis) directly in silicon. Hardware-accelerated formal synthesis will enable autonomous systems to dynamically verify and update neural barrier certificates in milliseconds as robots enter unfamiliar environments, unifying formal guarantees with continuous empirical discovery.
3. **Certificate-Preserving Edge PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning)**: In open-world deployment, robots must continually adapt to non-stationary environments, mechanical wear (gear backlash, thermal expansion), and novel non-rigid object geometries (cables, cloth, elastomeric seals). In classical machine learning, online adaptation continuously backpropagates gradients into model weights. But in Physical AI, updating weights $\theta \to \theta + \Delta \theta$ alters the proposal distribution, which instantly invalidates formal barrier certificates and resets the Poisson empirical exposure clock ($T \ge 3.0/\lambda$) to zero! Furthermore, on-device backpropagation triggers severe thermal throttling on sealed mobile platforms ($T_j \ge 105^\circ\text{C}$). Frontier MLSys architectures must develop certificate-preserving PEFT frameworks: parameter updates must be strictly confined to isolated task-adaptation sub-networks (such as low-rank LoRA adapters or prompt tokens) that operate within an unprivileged sandbox, mathematically decoupled from immutable, certified safety envelopes.
4. **Asynchronous Distributed Multi-Robot Consensus**: Coordinating heterogeneous fleets of autonomous mobile manipulators, aerial quadrotors, and human coworkers in shared industrial spaces breaks the assumption of centralized, shared-memory state estimation. In collaborative manipulation of non-rigid objects (such as two bipedal humanoids carrying a flexible sheet or long beam), internal tension forces couple the robots' dynamics across continuous physical space. Wireless packet loss, channel fading, and asymmetric network jitter ($20\text{ to }200\,\text{ms}$) create dynamic, decentralized epistemic horizons where every agent operates on stale, un-synchronized world representations. When multi-agent Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) enforce conservative pairwise collision avoidance, symmetric yield conditions frequently degenerate into fleet-wide deadlock freezes at physical intersections. Formulating decentralized, asynchronous safety-critical coordination protocols that guarantee liveness while enforcing hard collision invariance remains one of the preeminent open challenges of physical ML systems.

The running machine ends the book refused. On the book's evidence the adjudicator of @sec-release-case-worked-full signs `REFUSE` on all six claims, because each rests on a premise the records leave illustrative or unknown. The measurements of @tbl-16-cond-measurements would move that verdict only part of the way. Once they support the premises they settle, the most a release could sign is `COND` for a named part of the envelope, covering aisle travel in the `{python} OilFilm.v_restricted_str` restricted mode on inspected floors, the door at the guarded approach, and the handover to the coworker. The `{python} OilFilm.v_aisle_str` normal mode would stay unsigned, because it rests on the friction floor that the oil film leaves open. Under either verdict the three entries of @tbl-17-claims-register stay open, each with its owner and closure test, and all three are unmeasured observables that only a qualified detector can close: a floor-film detector, a qualified rack-end presence sensor, and a qualified identity check at the pick station. None of them is a scope mismatch or a theoretical deficit. The machine's authority stops where the register says it does.

::: {.callout-perspective title="The engineering resolution of refusal"}
A naive engineering team evaluates $1{,}000$ successful benchmark trials, signs `RELEASE` for $1.3\text{ m/s}$ normal mode, and encounters a catastrophic overrun the first time a pallet jack leaks hydraulic fluid onto an uninspected floor. Signing `REFUSE` on unverified normal mode while admitting a conditional restricted mode ($1.0\text{ m/s}$) on inspected floors is not a failure of robotics; it is the fundamental definition of engineering accountability. Refusing unverified authority delivers a dependable, accident-free system today while providing an explicit, funded engineering roadmap (the closure tests) to earn higher operational authority tomorrow.
:::

That verdict is the four laws applied to one machine, and the parcel induction cell carried the same laws through a machine the book had not examined. Each law also led one part of this book, and each part handed forward records that state their own conditions. Together those records carry the answer to the question the book opened with, and they also mark where that answer stops. @Fig-17-causal-loop-synthesis draws the loop they protect. The Brain proposes, the permission path admits or refuses each proposal against fresh state, and the Body delivers the admitted command across the Boundary into a World that keeps evolving whether or not any level observes it.
